about.text: This style guide provides editorial guidelines for writing clear and consistent technical documentation for an audience of software developers and other technical practitioners.

If you're new to the guide and looking for introductory topics about our style, then start with Highlights , Voice and tone , and Text-formatting summary . Otherwise, use the guide as a reference document for specific questions. For example, you can look up terms in the word list .

about.heading: Break the rules
about.text: —George Orwell, " Politics and the English Language "

about.heading: Break the rules
about.text: This guide contains guidelines, not rules. Depart from it when doing so improves your content.

about.heading: Break the rules
about.text: For example, if we recommend spelling a term as one word, and you determine that the hyphenated version of a term in your domain is more appropriate for your readers, then it's fine to use that instead. We acknowledge that sometimes there are competing forms of the same word in wide use, especially as new terms emerge, and you might have good reasons for departing from our guidance.

about.heading: Break the rules
about.text: When you depart from this guide, be consistent throughout your document.

highlights.text: The style guide covers a lot of material, so the following page provides an overview of its most important points. For more information about topics on the page, follow the links.

highlights.heading: Tone and content
highlights.text: Be conversational and friendly without being frivolous.

highlights.heading: Tone and content
highlights.text: Don't pre-announce anything in documentation.

highlights.heading: Tone and content
highlights.text: Use descriptive link text .

highlights.heading: Tone and content
highlights.text: Write accessibly .

highlights.heading: Tone and content
highlights.text: Write for a global audience .

highlights.heading: Language and grammar
highlights.text: Use second person : "you" rather than "we."

highlights.heading: Language and grammar
highlights.text: Use active voice : make clear who's performing the action.

highlights.heading: Language and grammar
highlights.text: Use standard American spelling and punctuation.

highlights.heading: Language and grammar
highlights.text: Put conditions before instructions , not after.

highlights.heading: Language and grammar
highlights.text: For usage and spelling of specific words, see the word list .

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Use sentence case for document titles and section headings.

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Use numbered lists for sequences.

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Use bulleted lists for most other lists.

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Use description lists for pairs of related pieces of data.

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Use serial commas .

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Put code-related text in code font .

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Put UI elements in bold .

highlights.heading: Formatting, punctuation, and organization
highlights.text: Use unambiguous date formatting .

highlights.heading: Images
highlights.text: Provide alt text .

highlights.heading: Images
highlights.text: Provide high-resolution or vector images when practical.

philosophy.text: This document discusses some of the principles and philosophy behind this style guide.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: This style guide codifies and records our style decisions and describes our house style. The guide doesn't claim to be objectively correct.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: This guide is not intended to do the following:

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: Compete with other well-known style guides.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: Replace another style guide that you already follow.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: Provide a complete set of basic writing guidelines.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: Provide legal advice. For legal advice, consult a lawyer.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: The guidance in this style guide doesn't limit the changes that Google can make to its documentation.

philosophy.heading: Intended purpose
philosophy.text: If you don't read a given guideline, then you are still responsible for behaving ethically and lawfully with regard to documentation.

philosophy.heading: Explanation of reasons for guidelines
philosophy.text: We generally don't explain the reasoning behind most of our guidelines. We have a couple of reasons for that:

philosophy.heading: Explanation of reasons for guidelines
philosophy.text: Many of our decisions are driven by accessibility, localization, globalization, and ease of understanding. Giving those reasons as explanations everywhere they apply would be repetitive.

philosophy.heading: Explanation of reasons for guidelines
philosophy.text: Often, a given guideline is one good option among several; in those cases, we sometimes just chose one option for consistency.

philosophy.heading: Explanation of reasons for guidelines
philosophy.text: Too much explanation can clutter up a page. Readers most often want a brief answer to a specific question, rather than a detailed explanation.

philosophy.heading: Explanation of reasons for guidelines
philosophy.text: That said, we recognize that it's sometimes useful to know why we made a given choice, so we've started to include occasional explanations in the What's new page.

word-list.text: This word list covers style and usage guidelines that are specific to developer documentation.

If the term that you're looking for isn't on this list, check our other editorial resources , including our preferred dictionary, Merriam-Webster . If there are multiple spellings in the Merriam-Webster word entry, use the first form listed, which is the most common spelling. For example, in the entry for cancel , the first form listed for the past tense is canceled , indicating that it's more common than cancelled .
If you're looking for a technical definition, then it's often a good idea to check the authoritative documentation on the topic.

Terminology decisions, including how and when to define or contextualize terms, often require judgments based on factors like your product area, your audience, and prevailing convention. Here are some other pages of this guide that can help you make those types of judgments:
Jargon
Inclusive language
Write for a global audience
Hyphens
Capitalization
As always, it's fine to deviate from our guidance if that serves your readers better. For more information, see Break the rules .

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: All word list entries have a link link icon next to them. To link directly to an entry, you can right-click and copy the link address, or click and copy the URL from your address bar.

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: Some word list entries include guidance to avoid or don't use a term. Apply this guidance as follows:

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: Use with caution . A recommendation to avoid using the term when possible , or to use the term with caution. The term might be ambiguous or obscure, so we provide alternative term suggestions or suggest that you use a more specific term. However, you can use the term if needed. Where appropriate, define the term or use it only once, as explained on the Jargon page.

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: Don't use . In all cases, we prefer to not use the term . The term might be particularly ambiguous or it might have an offensive or non-inclusive association. If such a term appears in code, we recommend that you replace or write around the term .

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: Android . Applies only to Android documentation.

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: Google Cloud . Applies only to Google Cloud documentation.

word-list.heading: Word list
word-list.text: Google Workspace . Applies only to Google Workspace documentation.

word-list.heading: Numbers and Symbols
word-list.text: + link: OK to use + with numbers in text, such as customer records with 300+ demographic attributes , except in formal contexts.

word-list.heading: Numbers and Symbols
word-list.text: & (ampersand) link: Don't use & instead of and in headings, text, navigation, or tables of contents. It's OK to use & when referencing UI elements that use & , or in table headings and diagram labels where space constraints require abbreviation. It's OK to use & for technical purposes in code.

word-list.heading: Numbers and Symbols
word-list.text: 2-Step Verification link: When referring to Google's 2-Step Verification , use initial caps. When referring to generic 2-step verification , use lowercase.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: a and an link: Use a when the next word starts with a consonant sound , regardless of what letter it starts with. For more information, see Articles (a, an, the) .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: A/B testing link: Capitalize and use slash notation for A/B .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: abnormal link: Don't use to refer to a person. OK to use to refer to a condition of a computer system.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: abort link: Avoid in general usage. Instead, use words like stop , exit , cancel , or end . In Linux, abort refers to a type of signal that terminates an abnormal process.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: about versus on link: When a cross-reference includes information that describes what the cross-reference links to, use about instead of on . Recommended : For more information about indexes, see Managing indexes . Not recommended : For more information on indexes, see Managing indexes .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: above link: Don't use for a range of version numbers. Instead, use later . Don't use to refer to a position in a document. Instead, use earlier or preceding . Don't use to refer to a position in the UI. Instead, write instructions that avoid directional language. For more information, see Writing accessible documentation . It's OK to use above in a non-directional way, such as when describing a hierarchy.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: access (verb) link: Avoid when you can. Instead, use friendlier words like see , edit , find , use , or view .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: access token link: Lowercase except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: account name link: Don't use. Instead, use username .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: actionable link: Avoid unless it's the clearest and simplest phrasing for your audience. Instead, leave it out or replace it with a phrase like that you can act on or useful . Don't use actionable in the legal sense without consulting a lawyer.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: action bar link: In Android documentation, don't use. Instead, use app bar .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: ad tech link: Write out on first mention: advertising technology (ad tech) . Don't use adtech or ad-tech .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: address bar link: Use to refer to the URL bar or the combined URL bar and search box in a browser. Don't use omnibox .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: ad hoc link: OK to use in database and analytics contexts to mean "free-form" or "user-written" (for example, ad hoc queries or an ad hoc chart ). For other contexts, try to find a more specific English equivalent. Don't hyphenate or italicize the term.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: admin link: Write out administrator unless it's the name of a UI label or other element. It's OK to use admin in Android documentation.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: administrator link: In Android documentation, don't use. Instead, use admin .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: advertised route priority link: OK to also use base advertised route priority when discussing region-to-region costs. Don't shorten or use variations of these terms.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: agnostic link: Don't use. Instead, use a more precise term like platform-independent .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: AI link: In general, you can use AI without spelling out artificial intelligence . Most readers are familiar with the abbreviation AI . If you think your audience isn't familiar with the term, spell it out on first use.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: aka link: Don't use. Instead, write out also known as , or present an alternative term using parentheses or the word or . You can also write out a definition. Recommended : Geographic data, also known as geospatial data, is ... Recommended : Geographic data (geospatial data) is ... Recommended : Geographic data, or geospatial data, is ...

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: all apps screen link: In Android documentation: Lowercase except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: allowlist (verb), allowlisted, allowlisting link: Don't use as a verb. Instead, rewrite to improve clarity. OK to use allowlist as a noun. For more information, see blacklist .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: allows you to link: Don't use. Instead, use lets you . For more information, see enable .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: alpha link: Lowercase except when part of a product name. Recommended : PRODUCT_NAME Alpha Recommended : PRODUCT_NAME is in alpha.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: America, American link: Use only to refer to the Americas or the American continent . Don't use to refer to the United States. Instead, use a more precise term like the US or the United States , and people in the US . For more information, see US .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: among link: See between versus among .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: AM, PM link: To be consistent with Material Design , use all caps, no periods, and a space before. Recommended : 9:00 AM Recommended : 10:30 PM

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: and/or link: Don't use unless space is limited, such as in a table. For more information, see Slashes .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: Android link: When referring to the operating system, capitalize Android .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: Android-powered device link: Not Android device .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: and so on link: Avoid using and so on whenever possible. For more information, see etc.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: anti* link: See guidance about hyphens with prefixes .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: anti-pattern link: Avoid using anti-pattern , particularly as a standalone heading. Instead, consider using a more specific and broadly understood term. Recommended : Avoid these five SQL errors. Recommended : Avoid these five programming practices that make SQL queries inefficient. Not recommended : Avoid these five SQL anti-patterns.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: API link: Use API to refer to either a web API or a language-specific API. Don't use API when referring to a method or a class. For example, don't write This resource has one API to mean "This resource has one method."

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: API Console, APIs console, developer console, dev console, or Google API Console link: Don't use. Instead, refer to the Google APIs Explorer or to the Google Cloud console . For more information, see console .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: API Console key link: In most contexts, use API key instead of API Console key . In Apps admin APIs, it's OK to use API Console key to distinguish from other API keys.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: API key link: Not developer key or dev key .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: APIs Explorer link: Not API explorer or other variants.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: app link: In general, use app instead of application when referring to programs for end users, especially in the context of mobile or web software. In some contexts, such as enterprise software, it's OK to use application to convey a sense of greater complexity. Use application in standard phrases such as application programming interface .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: app bar link: In Android contexts, formerly action bar .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: appendix link: Use the plural appendixes , not appendices .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: application link: See app .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: as link: If you mean because , then use because instead of as . As is ambiguous; it can refer to the passage of time. Because refers to causation or the reason for something.

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: as of this writing link: Avoid because this phrase is implied. The phrase can also prematurely disclose product or feature strategy or inappropriately imply that a product or feature might change. See also currently and presently . Recommended : BigQuery doesn't support that function. Not recommended : As of this writing, BigQuery doesn't support that function. For more information, see Timeless documentation .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: authentication and authorization link: In general, use the word authenticated only to refer to users, and use authorized only to refer to requests that are sent by a client app on behalf of an authenticated user. A user authenticates their identity by entering their password (or giving some other proof of identity). The authenticated user then authorizes the client app to send an authorized request to the server on the user's behalf. When you want to use a preposition with authenticate , use against .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: authN, authZ link: Don't use. Instead, use authentication or authorization .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: auto* link: See guidance about hyphens with prefixes .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: autohealing link: Not auto-healing .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: auto mode VPC network link: Not auto mode network .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: autopopulate link: Not auto populate or auto-populate .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: autoscaling link: Not auto-scaling .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: autotagging link: Not auto-tagging .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: autoupdate link: Don't use. Instead, use automatically update .

word-list.heading: A
word-list.text: -aware link: Avoid using as a compound modifier, as in healthcare-aware . OK to use when it's part of a product name, such as Identity-Aware Proxy .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: backend link: Not back-end or back end .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: bar link: Avoid when possible. For more information, see foo .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: bare metal link: Lowercase except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item. Hyphenate when used as a compound modifier, such as bare-metal server .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: base64 link: Lowercase except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item. Otherwise, capitalize Base64 only if it's part of a formal name. Write base64 in code font only if it's a string literal or otherwise quoted from code.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: baz link: Avoid when possible. For more information, see foo .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: below link: Don't use for a range of version numbers. Instead, use earlier . Don't use to refer to a position in a document. Instead, use later or following . Don't use to refer to a position in the UI. Instead, write instructions that avoid directional language. For more information, see Writing accessible documentation . It's OK to use below in set phrases such as below (the) average , below the mean , below zero . It's OK to use below in a non-directional way, such as when describing a hierarchy.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: best effort link: Avoid where possible. Instead, use more specific wording. After providing a description, you can add a phrase like "sometimes referred to as best effort ."

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: beta link: Lowercase except when part of a product name. Recommended : PRODUCT_NAME Beta Recommended : PRODUCT_NAME is currently in beta.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: between versus among link: It's fine to use between when talking about more than two things; however, between isn't interchangeable with among . Use between when you're talking about two or more distinct things: Recommended : JavaScript introduces dependencies between the DOM, the CSSOM, and JavaScript execution. Use among when you're talking about things that are part of a group or things that aren't distinct: Recommended : ... a conventional SQL database that can be shared among multiple apps. More examples: Recommended : Because screen dimensions vary widely among devices (for example, between phones and tablets, and even among different phones), you should configure the viewport so that your pages render correctly on many different devices. Not recommended : Because screen dimensions vary widely between devices (for example, between phones and tablets, and even between different phones), you should configure the viewport so that your pages render correctly on many different devices. Recommended : You can share services among multiple clients. Not recommended : You can share services between multiple clients. See also Grammar Girl's discussion of between and among .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: big-endian link: Hyphenate. Lowercase except at the beginning of a sentence, heading, or list item. Recommended : The codebase assumes big-endian byte ordering. Not recommended : The codebase assumes Big Endian byte ordering. Not recommended : The codebase assumes Big-endian byte ordering. Not recommended : The codebase assumes big endian byte ordering.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: billing charges link: Don't use billing charges to mean charges that appear on a bill. Instead, use billed charges . Use billing charges to describe the cost of creating the bill.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: black-box link: Avoid using black-box , blackbox , or black box to describe monitoring and testing. Consider using a more precise term for clarity. For monitoring, use synthetic monitoring . For testing, use opaque-box testing .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: Black Friday link: Avoid unless explicitly referring to an event in the US. Instead use peak scale event .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blackhat, black hat, black-hat link: Don't use. Instead, use precise terms for the kind of violation or practice, such as illegal , unethical , or in violation of rules .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blackhole (verb), blackholed (adjective) link: Don't use. Instead, use a more descriptive term or phrase, such as dropped without notification .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blacklist, black list, black-list link: Don't use blacklist , whitelist , and graylist . Instead, use more precise terms that are appropriate for your domain. For the noun blacklist , consider using a replacement such as denylist , excludelist , or blocklist . For the noun whitelist , consider using a replacement such as allowlist , trustlist , or safelist . For the noun graylist ( greylist ), consider using a replacement such as provisional list . In all of these cases, consider that there might not actually be a list involved. When replacing problematic terms, be sure to be technically accurate for the specific context. For the verb forms of these words, a simple word-for-word replacement typically isn't the best solution. Instead, replace verbs such as blacklisted with phrases that accurately convey the relevant action. For example: Recommended : To deny requests from an IP address, add it to the dos.yaml file. Not recommended : To denylist an IP address, add it to the dos.yaml file. Don't use : To blacklist an IP address, add it to the dos.yaml file. If the command or code that you're documenting uses one of these words, then use the words only in direct reference to the code items ( formatted as code ), and make it clear what you're referring to. Recommended : Add a user to the allowlist ( whitelist ) by entering the following: whitelist adduser EMAIL_ADDRESS . Not recommended : Add a user to the whitelist by entering the following: whitelist adduser EMAIL_ADDRESS . For more information, see the inclusive documentation page.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blacklisted, black listed, black-listed link: Don't use. See blacklist .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blacklisting, black listing, black-listing link: Don't use. See blacklist .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blast radius link: Don't use. Instead, use a more precise term like affected area or spatial impact .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blind link: Avoid using blind to or blind eye to . Instead, use more precise terms like ignore , unaware of , disregard , avoid , or reject . Avoid using blind writes . Instead, use a more precise phrase, such as a write operation without a read operation . Avoid using blind change or change blindly . Instead, use a more precise phrase such as change without first confirming the value . When referring to people, use terms like person who is blind , screen reader user (if applicable), person who is visually impaired , person who is low-vision , magnification user (if applicable).

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: blue-green link: Not blue/green or blue green .

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: boolean link: In most contexts, boolean refers to a specific data type in a specific programming language. In such cases, use code font and the exact spelling and capitalization of the programming keyword. When referring to the abstract data type, use lowercase. If you refer to Boolean mathematics or Boolean logic , use uppercase.

word-list.heading: B
word-list.text: branding information link: In the Google Cloud console, the phrase branding information refers to the information that Google shows to users when the client asks them to authorize access: specifically, the project's name and logo, and the developer's Google Account. This information is set in the Consent screen page.

word-list.heading: B

word-list.heading: H
word-list.text: happiness and satisfaction link: Use happiness when referring to a customer's perception of a site's reliability. Use satisfaction when referring to whether the site meets the customer's needs. Site reliability engineering (SRE) content generally refers to measuring customer happiness instead of customer satisfaction . The two phrases are not equivalent. The distinction the SRE documentation makes is between satisfying a need (a dispassionate act) and establishing an emotional response (creating happiness). Although it is difficult to measure happiness precisely, SRE uses service level indicators (SLIs) to quantify user perception. For example, a customer might feel a "need" to watch a show on TV. If the show is available, the customer's need is satisfied. But if playback is slow or choppy, the customer might not be happy. For more information about SRE and measuring reliability, see The Happiness Test .

product-names.text: This page describes how to use product names.

product-names.heading: Capitalize product names
product-names.text: In general, Google product names are in title case , sometimes called init-capped , which means that every word is capitalized except for prepositions like of or on and articles like a or the . When you refer to a Google product, use title case except when you're matching a UI label. For information about how to refer to UI labels, see UI elements and interaction .

product-names.heading: Capitalize product names
product-names.text: When you write about any product, follow the official capitalization for the names of brands, companies, software, products, services, features, and terms defined by companies and open source communities.

product-names.heading: Capitalize product names
product-names.text: For example, if you're using Kubernetes-related terms, then follow the capitalization that's shown in the Kubernetes Concepts documentation . Recommended in a Kubernetes context : A Job creates one or more Pods. Recommended : The Cloud Scheduler job publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic at one-minute intervals.

product-names.heading: Capitalize product names
product-names.text: If an official name begins with a lowercase letter, then put it in lowercase even at the start of a sentence. But it's better to revise the sentence to avoid putting a lowercase word at the start, if possible. Recommended : You can use macOS to run the app. Not recommended : macOS can run the app.

product-names.heading: Feature names
product-names.text: A feature is a distinctive attribute or capability of a product. Features are usually described in terms of what they can do as part of a product. In general, feature names are lowercase, although there are exceptions.

product-names.heading: Feature names
product-names.text: When you write about a feature, don't capitalize it unless the name is officially capitalized. If you're unsure, follow the precedent that's set by other documents that describe the feature. As with products, match the capitalization of a UI label if you're referring to one.

product-names.heading: Feature names
product-names.text: For more general information about capitalization, see Capitalization .

product-names.heading: Shorten Google product names
product-names.text: When referring to a Google product, sometimes you might want to abbreviate the product name. For example, when you're referring to Google Spreadsheets, it can be awkward to refer to it as Google Spreadsheets every time; sometimes you might want to call it Spreadsheets.

product-names.heading: Shorten Google product names
product-names.text: Use the full trademarked product name. Don't abbreviate product names, except in cases where you're matching a UI label. In such cases, make it clear that you're referring to the Google product and not some other thing with a similar name.

product-names.heading: Shorten Google product names
product-names.text: Also consider whether you need to refer to a product name throughout a document, or if you can use a more general term. For example, if you've established that you're talking about Anthos Service Mesh , you can probably frame your discussion around the concept of a service mesh throughout much of the document.

product-names.heading: Possessives of product names
product-names.text: For information about forming possessives with product names, see Product, feature, and company names .

product-names.heading: Articles before product names
product-names.text: Don't use the before a product name unless you're using the name to modify something else. Do use the before tool and API names.

product-names.text: It's OK to refer to Google products as services, such as the Google Kubernetes Engine service or the Compute Engine service . However, if the term services leads to ambiguity, use the product names.

text-formatting.text: The page summarizes, and provides a quick reference for, many of the general text-formatting conventions covered elsewhere in the style guide. For more information, see Visual formatting .

Bold: Use bold formatting, <b> or ** , only for UI elements and run-in headings , including at the beginning of notices . Although a double underscore, __ , can also indicate bold styling in Markdown, it can be difficult to distinguish in a text editor. It's best to use the double asterisk for bold in Markdown.

Italic: In general, use italics sparingly. When you're discussing or introducing terms, such as when defining terms or using words as words , use italics formatting, <i> or _ . For more information, see Use italics to discuss terms and Format abbreviation introductions . When you need to add emphasis to indicate importance, use italics, not bold or underline. But usually, your words can carry the emphasis without adding italics. To indicate semantic emphasis in HTML, use the em element, which renders as italics in most contexts. To indicate emphasis in Markdown, use underscores ( _ ), which render as italics; you can't do semantic tagging in Markdown. Although an asterisk, * , can also indicate italics in Markdown, we recommend underscores to make it easier for humans to distinguish italics from bold in the Markdown file. Italicize titles of books, movies, web series, and other full-length works, unless they're part of a link. For more information, see Cross-references and linking . Italicize mathematical variables—for example, x + y = 3. Don't italicize mathematical operators such as the plus sign. For more information about formatting mathematical notation, see Mathematical notation . Italicize version variables—for example, version 1.4. x .
Underline: Reserve underlining for link text. For more information, see Style link text .

Code font: Use <code> in HTML or ` in Markdown to apply a monospace font and other styling to code in text , inline code, and user input. Use code blocks, <pre> or ``` , for code samples or other blocks of code. Do not override or modify font styles inline. Use code font to mark up code, such as filenames, class names, method names, HTTP status codes, console output, and placeholders. For more information, see Some specific items to put in code font .
Capitalization: Use American English style for general capitalization . Use sentence case in all headings, titles, and navigation . Use all-capitals for placeholders .

Quotation marks: In general, use American English style when punctuating quotations . For titles of shorter works—such as articles or episodes in a web series—put titles in quotation marks, unless they're part of a link.

Font type, size, and color: Do not override global styles for font type, size, or color . Use semantic HTML or Markdown to control the style of text on a page—for example, code tags in HTML ( <code> ) or backticks in Markdown ( ` )—instead of manually styling text with a monospace font.

Other punctuation conventions: Don't use ampersands (&) as conjunctions or shorthand for and . Use and instead. That includes headings and navigation. Exception : It's okay to use & in cases where you need to refer to a UI element or the name of a menu that uses & . Put quotation marks and end punctuation outside of link text. For more information, see the Punctuation around link text and Quotation marks and italics sections of the "Cross-references and linking" page.

accessibility.text: We write our developer documentation with accessibility in mind. This page is not an exhaustive reference, but describes some general guidelines and examples that illustrate best practices to follow. The World Health Organization estimates that 15% of the world's population (more than 1 billion people) have an accessibility need. When documentation is written with accessibility in mind, it improves the overall experience for all readers.
For other writing best practices, see the following resources:
Write for a global audience
Write inclusive documentation
Voice and tone

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Don't use ableist language. Avoid bias and harm when discussing disability and accessibility. For more information, see Writing inclusive documentation .

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Ensure that readers can reach all parts of the document (including tabs, form-submission buttons, and interactive elements) by using only a keyboard, without a mouse or trackpad.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Use a screen reader to test your documentation. This test can help you find accessibility issues in your content and is a good way to self-edit your content. To try out a screen reader, see List of screen readers .

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: In HTML, use semantic tagging . For example, use the em element only to indicate emphasis, not to indicate italics.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: In HTML, prefer native elements over custom styles.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Avoid unnecessary font formatting. (Screen readers explicitly describe text modifications.)

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: If you're documenting a product that includes specialized accessibility features, then explicitly document those features. For example, the Google Cloud CLI ( gcloud CLI) includes togglable accessibility features such as percentage progress bars and ASCII box rendering.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Don't force line breaks (hard returns) within sentences and paragraphs. Line breaks might not work well in resized windows or with enlarged text.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Avoid when possible camel case and all caps . Some screen readers read capitalized letters individually, and some languages are unicase . Follow capitalization guidelines.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Depending on the screen reader (or personal settings), not all punctuation marks are read. Make sure that the same meaning is conveyed to the reader without punctuation marks. For that reason, avoid when possible the use of exclamation marks, question marks, and semicolons.

accessibility.heading: General dos and don'ts
accessibility.text: Don't use & instead of and in headings, text, navigation, or tables of contents. However, it's OK to use & when referencing UI elements that use & , or in table headings and diagram labels where space constraints require abbreviation. Of course, it's fine to use & for technical purposes in code.

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Break up walls of text to aid in scannability. For example, separate paragraphs , create headings , and use lists .

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Use shorter sentences. Try to use fewer than 26 words per sentence.

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Define acronyms and abbreviations on first usage and if they're used infrequently.

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Use parallel writing structures for similar things. For example, start each list in the same format.

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Place distinguishing and important information of a paragraph in the first sentence to aid in scannability.

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Use clear and direct language. Avoid the use of double negatives and exceptions for exceptions. Recommended : You can continue without a path. Not recommended : A missing path won't prevent you from continuing.

accessibility.heading: Ease of reading
accessibility.text: Left-align text for readability. Don't center or full-justify text.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: Use descriptive headings and titles because they help a reader navigate their browser and the page. It's easier to jump between pages and sections of a page if the headings and titles are unique.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: Use a heading hierarchy.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: Don't skip levels of the heading hierarchy. For example, put an h3 element only after an h2 element.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: To change the visual formatting of a heading, use CSS rather than using a heading level that doesn't fit the hierarchy.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: Don't have empty headings or headings with no associated content.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: Tag headings using heading elements. In HTML: h1 , h2 , and so on. In Markdown: # , ## , and so on.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: Use a level-1 heading for the page title or main content heading.

accessibility.heading: Headings and titles
accessibility.text: For more information and examples, see Headings and titles .

accessibility.heading: Links
accessibility.text: Use meaningful link text . Links should make sense when read out of context.

accessibility.heading: Links
accessibility.text: Don't use click here or read this document . Some people who use screen readers jump from link to link to scan a page and need to understand what a link contains.

accessibility.heading: Links
accessibility.text: Use see to refer to links and cross-references. For more information, see see .

accessibility.heading: Links
accessibility.text: When a link does anything that the reader might not expect, such as downloading a file, opening in a new tab, or jumping to another section on the same page, explain that behavior when you link. For more information, see Explain unexpected link behavior .

accessibility.heading: Links
accessibility.text: When possible, avoid adjacent links. Instead, put a character in between to separate them.

accessibility.heading: Lists
accessibility.text: In a procedure , make each instruction a list item .

accessibility.heading: Lists
accessibility.text: Use lists to make it easier for the reader to follow the steps.

accessibility.heading: Images
accessibility.text: For every image, provide an alt attribute. For alt attributes that contain alt text , use alt text that adequately summarizes the intent of each image. If the image is purely decorative, use empty alt text.

accessibility.heading: Images
accessibility.text: Don't present new information in images. Always provide an equivalent text explanation with the image.

accessibility.heading: Images
accessibility.text: Don't repeat images unless absolutely necessary.

accessibility.heading: Images
accessibility.text: Don't use images of text, code samples, or terminal output. Use actual text.

accessibility.heading: Images
accessibility.text: Use SVG instead of PNG if available. SVGs stay sharp when you zoom in on the image.

accessibility.heading: Images
accessibility.text: For more information, see Text associated with images .

accessibility.heading: Videos, recordings, and GIFs
accessibility.text: Provide captions, transcripts, or descriptions of audio and video content. For example, you can use the autocaption feature in YouTube.

accessibility.heading: Videos, recordings, and GIFs
accessibility.text: Ensure that captions can be translated into major languages.

accessibility.heading: Videos, recordings, and GIFs
accessibility.text: Don't use flickering or flashing elements. They can cause anything from motion sickness to a seizure.

accessibility.heading: Buttons and icons
accessibility.text: For form-submission buttons, use the native HTML button element.

accessibility.heading: Buttons and icons
accessibility.text: An icon is a symbol or image that represents an object or a function. For information about using icons, see the Buttons and icons section of the "UI elements and interaction" page.

accessibility.heading: UI navigation
accessibility.text: When you use angle brackets ( > ) to document menu paths, add an aria-label attribute to help screen readers interpret the brackets as "and then" instead of as "greater than" or "keyboard arrow right". For more information and examples, see Menu bar .

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: Introduce tables in the text preceding the table because not all screen readers preannounce tables.

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: Use table headings for the first column and the first row only. Use the th element .

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: If your tables include both row and column headings, then mark heading cells with the scope attribute .

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: If your tables have more than one row containing column headings, then use the headers attribute and make sure that the headings have unique IDs.

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: Avoid when possible tables in the middle of a numbered procedure.

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: Don't merge cells. Don't use colspan or rowspan attributes.

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: Don't use tables unless it's the best method to present your information. Tables are challenging for screen readers. For more information, see List or table .

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: Don't present new information in tables through images or symbols alone; always provide a descriptive alt attribute for the image or symbol. For more information, see Alt text .

accessibility.heading: Tables
accessibility.text: For more information, see Tables .

accessibility.heading: Interactive elements
accessibility.text: Introduce an interactive element (such as a button that expands and collapses) in the text preceding the element.

accessibility.heading: Interactive elements
accessibility.text: Recommended if practical : To see a list of requirements, expand the Requirements section.

accessibility.heading: Interactive elements
accessibility.text: Recommended : To see a list of requirements, click the arrow_right expander arrow.

accessibility.heading: Forms
accessibility.text: Label every input field by using a label element.

accessibility.heading: Forms
accessibility.text: Place labels outside of fields.

accessibility.heading: Forms
accessibility.text: When you're creating an error message for form validation, clearly state what went wrong and how to fix it—for example: "Name is a required field."

accessibility.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
accessibility.text: Try to use your site's standard styles and standard JavaScript code as much as possible. However, if you do use custom styles or code, then follow these guidelines:

accessibility.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
accessibility.text: Pick colors that respect accessible color contrast ratios (4.5:1 for text).

accessibility.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
accessibility.text: Don't use visibility:hidden or display:none . Both styles hide information from screen readers.

accessibility.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
accessibility.text: Avoid when possible using mouseover events. But if you do use them, then add alternate focus and blur events for keyboard users.

accessibility.heading: Custom CSS and JavaScript
accessibility.text: Ensure that any ordering and positioning defined in styles reflects the DOM and the reading order (such as left to right and top to bottom) of your page.

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Make sure that your document conveys all the information that you intended when you view it in the following contexts:

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Without sound

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Using only sound

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Without images, including animation

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Without color

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Using a keyboard

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: With screen magnification

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Without punctuation

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Don't use color, size, location, or other visual cues as the primary way of communicating information.

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: If you're using color, an icon, or outline thickness to convey state, then also provide a secondary cue, such as a change in the text label.

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Refer to buttons and other elements by their label. For visual elements that have no text, don't try to describe the element. Instead, use the element's aria-label attribute if possible. For example: Recommended : Click Save . Recommended : Click Notifications . Not recommended : Click the bell icon.

accessibility.heading: Document rendering
accessibility.text: Don't use directional language to orient the reader, such as above , below , or right-hand side . This type of language doesn't work well for accessibility or for localization reasons. For example, what's on the right side for left-to-right languages appears on the left side for right-to-left languages. Don't use directional language to refer to a position in a document. For example, the text isn't below if it's being read by a screen reader. Instead, use earlier , preceding , or following . Recommended : In the preceding diagram, clients run jobs on multi-team or single-team clusters. Not recommended : In the diagram above, clients run jobs on multi-team or single-team clusters. If a UI element is hard to find, provide a screenshot . Recommended : Click menu Menu . Not recommended : In the left-side panel, click the button with three lines.
