abbreviations.text: Abbreviations include acronyms, initialisms, shortened words, and contractions.
In most contexts, the technical distinction between acronyms and initialisms isn't relevant; it's fine to use the word acronym to refer to both.
An acronym is formed from the first letters of words in a phrase, but is pronounced as if it were a word itself:
NATO for North Atlantic Treaty Organization
scuba for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus
An initialism is also formed from the first letters of words in a phrase, but each letter is pronounced separately:
CIA for Central Intelligence Agency
FYI for For Your Information
PR for Public Relations
A shortened word is just part of a word or phrase, sometimes with a period at the end:
Dr. for doctor
etc. for et cetera
min for minutes
CA for California
Contractions are discussed in a separate page of this style guide.

abbreviations.heading: Long and short versions of a word
abbreviations.text: Some words have a long version and a short version—for example:

abbreviations.heading: Long and short versions of a word
abbreviations.text: application and app

abbreviations.heading: Long and short versions of a word
abbreviations.text: demonstration and demo

abbreviations.heading: Long and short versions of a word
abbreviations.text: synchronize and sync

abbreviations.heading: Long and short versions of a word
abbreviations.text: The short versions of the words are not abbreviations, and if you use them, you don't need to put a period after them.

abbreviations.heading: Long and short versions of a word
abbreviations.text: If you're not sure whether a word is an abbreviation or just a short version of a longer word, look in our list of resources . If that doesn't settle the issue, use the speaking test: if you speak the short version as a word ( This is a demo version of the product ), you can usually treat it as a word and not an abbreviation.

abbreviations.heading: When to use abbreviations
abbreviations.text: Abbreviations are intended to save the writer and the reader time. If the reader has to think about an abbreviation, it can slow down their reading comprehension.

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: Use standard acronyms and initialisms that will save the reader time.

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: Spell out abbreviations on first reference. For more information, see When to spell out a term .

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: Avoid using abbreviations for terms that aren't related to the main topic of the document.

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: In the following examples, the main topic of the document is the internet of things, so low Earth orbit should not be abbreviated.

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: Recommended : The internet of things (IoT) service can even be used for connecting to sensors in low Earth orbit.

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: Not recommended : The IoT (internet of things) service can even be used for connecting to sensors in LEO (low Earth orbit).

abbreviations.heading: General dos and don'ts
abbreviations.text: Be wary of using specialized abbreviations that your readers might not understand. For more information about when to use such language, see Jargon .

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: In general, when an abbreviation is likely to be unfamiliar to the audience, spell it out upon first mention and include the abbreviation in parentheses immediately following.

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: Recommended : Border Gateway Protocol ( BGP )

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: For all subsequent mentions of the abbreviation, use the abbreviation by itself. If you use an abbreviation only once, include it only if you think the abbreviation is as commonly used as the spelled-out term. Otherwise, don't include the abbreviation.

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: If the first mention of a term occurs in a heading or title , you can use the abbreviation and then spell out the abbreviation in the first paragraph that follows the heading or title.

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: When deciding to spell out a term, consider your audience. If your document is going to be translated, spelling out a term can provide important context for both human and machine translation. It can also be helpful for readers who aren't as familiar with English. If the majority of your audience is likely to recognize and understand the term, then you don't need to spell it out. For example, if you're writing documentation for developers that references an API, you don't need to spell out application programming interface . However, if you're explaining the general concept of an API to someone with no programming experience, spelling out the abbreviation can be helpful.

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: In some cases, spelling out a term doesn't help the reader understand the term. For example, writing out portable document format doesn't help the reader understand what a PDF document is. In those cases, don't spell out the term.

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: The following abbreviations rarely need to be spelled out:

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: API

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: DVD

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: File formats such as PDF or XML

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: HTML

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: RAM

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: REST

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: Units of measurement such as MB, MiB, GB, or GiB

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: URL

abbreviations.heading: When to spell out a term
abbreviations.text: USB

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: When you spell out a term and include its abbreviation in parentheses, do the following:

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Italicize both the spelled-out term and its abbreviation.

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: In the following examples, the only difference is the italicization of BGP :

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Recommended : Establish Border Gateway Protocol ( BGP ) sessions using a router on the peer network.

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Not recommended : Establish Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) sessions using a router on the peer network.

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Capitalize the spelled-out version of the abbreviation only if the long form is a proper noun or is conventionally capitalized.

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: That is, don't capitalize the term only because the abbreviation includes capital letters.

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Recommended : data manipulation language (DML)

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Not recommended : Data Manipulation Language (DML)

abbreviations.heading: Format abbreviation introductions
abbreviations.text: Include the abbreviation in link text .

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: Don't use i.e. or e.g. ; instead, use that is or for example , respectively. For more information, see e.g. and i.e.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: It's okay to use etc. in some circumstances , but it's best to use different phrasing in most lists. For more information, see Comma-separated lists .

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: Don't use internet slang abbreviations such as tl;dr , ymmv , RTFM , or others. Write out what you mean in a non-figurative way.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: Use the most common form of a word. If the spelled-out word is common and easily understandable, use that rather than abbreviating. For example, write approximately instead of approx.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: Spell out shortened words or common symbols that are substitutions for words.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: Recommended : Updating the software made throughput 10 times faster.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations not to use
abbreviations.text: Not recommended : Updating the software made throughput 10x faster.

abbreviations.heading: Periods with abbreviations
abbreviations.text: Follow these guidelines:

abbreviations.heading: Periods with abbreviations
abbreviations.text: Don't use periods with acronyms or initialisms.

abbreviations.heading: Periods with abbreviations
abbreviations.text: Put a period at the end of a shortened word, except for date and time abbreviations.

abbreviations.heading: Periods with abbreviations
abbreviations.text: If you write or say an abbreviation as a word (for example, app or sync ), don't put a period after it.

abbreviations.heading: Periods with abbreviations
abbreviations.text: Don't use a period with an abbreviation for the name of a country, US state, or the District of Columbia (DC).

abbreviations.heading: Plural abbreviations
abbreviations.text: For guidance about how to make abbreviations plural, see Pluralization .

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations as verbs
abbreviations.text: Don't use acronyms, initialisms, or shortened words as verbs.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations as verbs
abbreviations.text: Recommended : Use SSH to log in to your remote shell.

abbreviations.heading: Abbreviations as verbs
abbreviations.text: Not recommended : Then ssh into your remote shell.

abbreviations.heading: Indefinite articles before abbreviations
abbreviations.text: Whether to use a or an before a term depends on the pronunciation of the term: use a before any consonant sound and an before any vowel sound. Pronunciation of abbreviations can vary, so in general, base your decision on the pronunciation that's most common for your audience.

abbreviations.heading: Indefinite articles before abbreviations
abbreviations.text: In particular, our word list includes preferences for " a SQL ", " a FHIR ", and " an SAP ".

abbreviations.heading: Indefinite articles before abbreviations
abbreviations.text: For more information about articles, see Articles .

voice.text: In general, use active voice (in which the grammatical subject of the sentence is the person or thing performing the action) instead of passive voice (in which the grammatical subject of the sentence is the person or thing being acted upon), although there are exceptions. Make clear who's performing the action.

In passive voice, it's easy to neglect to indicate who or what is performing a particular action. In this kind of construction, it's often hard for readers to figure out who's supposed to do something (such as the reader, the computer, the server, an end user, or a visitor to a web page).
Recommended : Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.
Not recommended : The service is queried, and an acknowledgment is sent.

It's possible to indicate who's performing the action in passive voice (using by ), but the resulting prose is generally not as good as if you were to recast the sentence as active voice. So whenever possible, make the doer the subject of the sentence.
Recommended : Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.
Not recommended : The service is queried by you, and an acknowledgment is sent by the server.
For more information, see Active voice vs. passive voice in Google's Technical Writing One guide.

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: In certain cases, it's okay to use passive voice. For example, passive can be okay in the following instances:

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: To emphasize an object over an action.

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: To de-emphasize a subject or actor.

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: Recommended : Over 50 conflicts were found in the file.

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: Not recommended : You created over 50 conflicts in the file.

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: If your readers don't need to know who's responsible for the action.

voice.heading: Exceptions
voice.text: Recommended : The database was purged in January.

anthropomorphism.text: Don't attribute human qualities to software or hardware.

Anthropomorphism is a category of figurative language, which is less precise and is often harder to understand and translate than direct language. For more information, see Write for a global audience .
Recommended : A Delimiter object specifies where to split a string.
Not recommended : A Delimiter object tells the splitter where a string should be broken.
Recommended : The PC detects a new device.
Not recommended : The PC sees a new device.

articles.text: For ease of comprehension and translation, include definite and indefinite articles ( a , an , and the ) in your writing. Don't skip articles for brevity, including in headings and titles.
For more information about using standard English word order and about writing for a global audience in general, see Write for a global audience .
For more information about writing clear headings and titles, see Headings and titles .
For information about using articles before product names, see Articles before product names .
For information about using a or an before an abbreviation when the pronunciation of the abbreviation can vary, see Indefinite articles before abbreviations .

capitalization.text: Follow the standard capitalization rules for American English. Additionally, do the following:
Don't use unnecessary capitalization; before you capitalize a word, think about why (and whether) it should be capitalized.

Don't rely on a difference in capitalization to convey meaning. For example, although people who are familiar with Kubernetes probably understand that a capitalized Pod is a Kubernetes unit, and a lowercase pod is any other kind of pod, that distinction is likely lost on many casual readers or those who are new to the domain.
Don't use all-uppercase, except in the following contexts: in official names, in abbreviations that are always written in all-caps, or when referring to code that uses all-caps.
Don't use camel case , except in official names or when referring to code that uses camel case.
For information about how to capitalize specific words, see the word list .

capitalization.heading: Capitalize product names
capitalization.text: For information about how to capitalize product names, see Product names .

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in titles and headings
capitalization.text: In document titles and headings , use sentence case. That is, capitalize only the first word in the title, the first word in a subheading after a colon, and any proper nouns or other terms that are always capitalized a certain way.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in titles and headings
capitalization.text: Even though you're using sentence case, don't put a period at the end of a title or heading.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in references to titles and headings
capitalization.text: In references to any title or heading from a document that follows this guide, use sentence case even if the title or heading itself uses title case. That way, when the title or heading is eventually updated to sentence case, the reference will match.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in references to titles and headings
capitalization.text: When you reference the title of any work or source that doesn't follow this guide, retain the original capitalization. For more information about internal and external references, see Cross-references and linking . For more information about formatting references to third-party sources, see HTML and semantic tagging .

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in references to titles and headings
capitalization.text: For more information about internal and external references, see Cross-references and linking .

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in references to titles and headings
capitalization.text: For more information about formatting references to third-party sources, see HTML and semantic tagging .

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and colons
capitalization.text: Use a lowercase letter to begin the first word of the text immediately following a colon, unless the text is one of the following:

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and colons
capitalization.text: A proper noun ( Open source software: Hadoop )

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and colons
capitalization.text: A heading; see also Capitalization in titles and headings

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and colons
capitalization.text: A quotation ( Arthurian wit: "Bring me yon sworde" )

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and colons
capitalization.text: Text that follows a label such as Caution or Note

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and figures
capitalization.text: Use sentence case for captions. Use sentence case for labels, callouts, and other text in images and diagrams.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in glossaries and indexes
capitalization.text: Use lowercase for glossary and index terms unless the term is a proper noun or has another reason to require capitalization.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in glossaries and indexes
capitalization.text: Use sentence case for glossary definitions.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization and hyphenated words
capitalization.text: When a hyphenated word is the first word in a sentence or in a heading, capitalize only the first element in the word, unless a subsequent element is a proper noun or proper adjective.

capitalization.heading: Capitalization in lists
capitalization.text: Use sentence case for items in all types of lists. For more information, see Capitalization and end punctuation .

capitalization.heading: Capitalization for tables in text
capitalization.text: Use sentence case for all the elements in a table: contents, headings, labels, and captions.

capitalization.heading: Special capitalization style names
capitalization.text: Don't use a casing style name, such as camel case or snake case , to describe a casing style. These names don't localize well and they aren't standardized. Instead, explain what the requirements are and provide an example.

capitalization.heading: Special capitalization style names
capitalization.text: Recommended : Enter the value for the attribute field in the format where there are no spaces between words and the first letter of each word is capitalized—for example, AssertionAccount .

contractions.text: In general, we write our documentation in an informal tone , so we recommend using common two-word contractions such as you're , don't , and there's .

contractions.heading: Negation contractions
contractions.text: In particular, we recommend using negation contractions such as isn't , don't , and can't . It's easy for a reader to miss the word not when they're scanning, whereas it's harder to misread don't as do .

contractions.heading: Negation contractions
contractions.text: If you need to emphasize the negative, you can use text formatting such as is not , which renders as "is not ." But in most cases, you don't need emphasis to make your point clear.

contractions.heading: Contractions to avoid
contractions.text: Don't make up nonstandard contractions such as guides're or browser's (where 's means is ).

contractions.heading: Contractions to avoid
contractions.text: Don't use three-word contractions such as mightn't've .

pluralization.text: In general, follow the standard rules for pluralization in US English and use the regular plural form of a word in most cases. Avoid using 's to form a plural to avoid confusing a plural with a possessive or contraction.
For more information, see Contractions and Possessives .

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: For sentences with long or complex subjects, make sure to use either a plural or singular appropriately.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : Confirm that the number of entries listed in the directory is accurate.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : The workloads with the app: backend label represent the traffic source.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Not recommended : The efficiency of algorithms that process data sets depend on memory allocation.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: For sentences with more than one subject being connected by and or or , make sure to use either a plural and singular appropriately.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : The request payload and header information are logged for debugging.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : Either the API keys or service account wasn't authenticated.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Not recommended : User authentication and authorization is processed and handled by the security module.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: For consistent style, use a plural after one or more , not a singular.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Because one or more can express the possibility of one or more outcomes, it's sometimes helpful to reword the sentence for clarity.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : If one or more tests fail, a system warning is triggered.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : If any one test fails, a system warning is triggered.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: See also Plurals in parentheses .

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Use a singular after more than one , not a plural.

pluralization.heading: Singular and plural
pluralization.text: Recommended : You can create more than one instance at a time.

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: In general, treat acronyms, initialisms, and other abbreviations as regular words when making them plural. Avoid using 's to form the plural to help distinguish the plural form from the possessive. For more information, see Possessives .

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : APIs, SKEs, and IDEs

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Not recommended : API's, SKE's, and IDE's

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: If the acronym, initialism, or abbreviation ends in s , sh , ch , or x , then add es —for example, OSes , DISHes , DCCHes , and BMXes .

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: When spelling out a term, make sure that both the spelled-out term and abbreviation match, with both either being a plural or singular.

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : virtual machines (VMs)

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Not recommended : virtual machines (VM)

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: When using numbers with units of measure, use the singular when spelling out the unit if the number is one. Otherwise, use the plural form for all other numbers, including zero, decimal numbers, and numbers greater than one.

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : 0 degrees

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : 0.5 degrees

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : 1 degree

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : 15 degrees

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Don't make an abbreviation plural when used as a unit with a number.

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Recommended : 64 GB

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Not recommended : 64 GBs

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: Make sure to include a space, preferably a nonbreaking space, between the number and abbreviation. For more information, see Spaces in units of measurement .

pluralization.heading: Plural abbreviations
pluralization.text: For more information, see Abbreviations .

pluralization.heading: Plural product and feature names
pluralization.text: In general, don't form a plural or possessive for the trademark of a product, feature, or company name. For more information, see Use trademarks only as modifiers and Product, feature, and company names .

pluralization.heading: Plural product and feature names
pluralization.text: In general, use singular class names. Don't manually make a singular class name plural. Doing so might cause issues in translation. Instead, add a plural noun after the class name.

pluralization.heading: Plural product and feature names
pluralization.text: Recommended : Intent objects and Activity instances

pluralization.heading: Plural product and feature names
pluralization.text: Not recommended : Intent s and Activity s

pluralization.heading: Plural product and feature names
pluralization.text: Not recommended : Intents and Activities

pluralization.heading: Plural product and feature names
pluralization.text: For more information, see API reference code comments .

pluralization.heading: Plurals in parentheses
pluralization.text: Don't put optional plurals in parentheses. Instead, use either a plural or singular construction and keep things consistent throughout your documentation. Choose what is most appropriate for your documentation and your audience. If it's important in a specific context to indicate both, use one or more .

pluralization.heading: Plurals in parentheses
pluralization.text: Recommended Not recommended

pluralization.heading: Plurals in parentheses
pluralization.text: To find your API key, visit the Credentials page. To find your API key(s), visit the Credentials page.

pluralization.heading: Plurals in parentheses
pluralization.text: The value of the parent depends on the values of its children. The value of the parent depends on the value(s) of its child(ren).

pluralization.heading: Plurals in parentheses
pluralization.text: You can use a physical linecard, which can contain one or more ports. You can use a physical linecard, which can contain port(s).

pluralization.heading: Plural pronouns
pluralization.text: For information about plural pronouns like we , you , and they , see Pronouns and Second person and first person .

possessives.text: In general, to form a possessive, follow these guidelines.
For singular nouns, including those that end in s , add 's to the end of the word.
Recommended : Modify each vector's record.
Recommended : Raise the storage class's quota.
For plural nouns that end in s , add only an apostrophe to the end of the word.
Recommended : Extend the models' capabilities.
Not recommended : Extend the models's capabilities.
For plural nouns that don't end in s , add 's to the end of the word.
If a possessive seems awkward, rewrite the sentence to omit the possessive.
Recommended : Analyze the business data.
Not recommended : Analyze the businesses' data.
Recommended : The rule that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued.
Not recommended : The Federal Trade Commission's (FTC's) rule.
Avoid using 's to form a plural noun. For more information, see Pluralization .

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: When describing function or performance, don't form a possessive from a feature name, product name, or trademark, regardless of who owns it. Instead, use the name as a modifier or rewrite to use a word like of to indicate the relationship.

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: Recommended : You can use this template to monitor Google Search performance.

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: Recommended : You can use this template to monitor the performance of Google Search.

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: Not recommended : You can use this template to monitor Google Search's performance.

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: To form the possessive of a company name, add 's to the end of the name. Don't form the possessive of a company name when using it as a trademark.

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: Recommended : Google's new office is nearby.

possessives.heading: Product, feature, and company names
possessives.text: Not recommended : The capabilities of Google's Search are vast.

possessives.heading: Code items
possessives.text: Don't form the possessive of a code item. Instead, form the possessive from the noun that follows the code item or rewrite to avoid the possessive form.

possessives.heading: Code items
possessives.text: Recommended : Compare the number to the wordCount method's return value.

possessives.heading: Code items
possessives.text: Recommended : Compare the number to the value returned by the wordCount method.

possessives.heading: Code items
possessives.text: Not recommended : Compare the number to wordCount 's return value.

possessives.heading: Code items
possessives.text: For more information, see Grammatical treatment of code elements .

prepositions.text: There's no rule against placing a preposition at the end of a sentence. Place the preposition where it makes the most sense and makes the sentence easiest to read. Use prepositions as needed, even at the ends of sentences.
Recommended : For details, see the client library documentation for the language you're interacting with.
Not recommended : For details, see the client library documentation for the language with which you're interacting.
Include prepositions that increase clarity, omit unnecessary prepositions, and don't clutter the sentence with too many prepositions.
Recommended : The icon for the connector manager turns green within a few minutes, and the connector instance is displayed shortly after.
For information about which preposition to use when referring to UI elements, see UI elements and interaction .

tense.text: Use present tense for statements that describe general behavior that's not associated with a particular time.
Recommended : Send a query to the service. The server sends an acknowledgment.
Not recommended : Send a query to the service. The server will send an acknowledgment.
However, it's fine to use future tense ( will ) to distinguish an action that will occur in the future.
Recommended : Add the filename to the backup list. The file will be archived the next time the backup process runs.
In the following example, future tense is appropriate because Pub/Sub sends messages asynchronously; messages are not received immediately by subscribers.
Recommended : A message is sent that will notify any Pub/Sub subscribers.
Not recommended : A message is sent that notifies any Pub/Sub subscribers.

Don't use future tense to describe how a product or feature will work after the next release or update. For more information, see Document future features . Also avoid the hypothetical future would —for example: Recommended : If you send an unsubscribe message, the server removes you from the mailing list. Not recommended : You can send an unsubscribe message. The server would then remove you from the mailing list.
Also avoid the hypothetical future would —for example:
Recommended : If you send an unsubscribe message, the server removes you from the mailing list.
Not recommended : You can send an unsubscribe message. The server would then remove you from the mailing list.

pronouns.text: Ensure that a pronoun clearly refers to its antecedent (the noun that it's replacing).

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Avoid vague and confusing references between a pronoun and its antecedent.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Recommended : If you type text in the field, the text doesn't change.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Not recommended : If you type text in the field, it doesn't change.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Recommended : The name of the function to execute in the given script. The name does not include parentheses or parameters.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Not recommended : The name of the function to execute in the given script. It does not include parentheses or parameters.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: In many cases, it's best to follow a demonstrative pronoun (like this and these ) with a noun.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Recommended : Set this value to true.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Not recommended : Set this to true.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Recommended : These approaches are your best options.

pronouns.heading: Ambiguous pronoun references
pronouns.text: Not recommended : These are your best options.

pronouns.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
pronouns.text: Don't use gender-specific pronouns unless the person you're referring to is actually that gender.

pronouns.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
pronouns.text: In particular, don't use he , him , his , she , or her as gender-neutral pronouns, and don't use he/she or (s)he or other such punctuational approaches. Instead, use the singular they .

pronouns.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
pronouns.text: Singular they has been in use for a long time; for example, Jane Austen used it , and in 2015 the Washington Post adopted it as part of their official style .

pronouns.heading: Gender-neutral pronouns
pronouns.text: For more suggestions, see The Chicago Manual of Style , 16th edition, section 5.225, "Nine techniques for achieving gender neutrality."

pronouns.heading: Optional pronouns
pronouns.text: To avoid ambiguity and clarify meaning in sentences, use optional pronouns such as that and which .

pronouns.heading: Optional pronouns
pronouns.text: Recommended Not recommended

pronouns.heading: Optional pronouns
pronouns.text: Right-click the link that you want to open. Right-click the link you want to open.

pronouns.heading: Optional pronouns
pronouns.text: You can use other option parameters, which are described in the following section. You can use other option parameters, described in the following section.

pronouns.heading: Optional pronouns
pronouns.text: For more information, see Relative pronouns .

pronouns.heading: Personal pronouns
pronouns.text: Avoid first-person pronouns ( I , we , us , our , and ours ) except in the following contexts:

pronouns.heading: Personal pronouns
pronouns.text: The questions in FAQs.

pronouns.heading: Personal pronouns
pronouns.text: A document whose author makes comments in the first person.

pronouns.heading: Personal pronouns
pronouns.text: Using we to refer to your organization, after using your organization's name. For example, "Example Pet Store recommends that you feed your aardvark Standardized Aardvark Treats. We cannot guarantee the happiness of your aardvark otherwise."

pronouns.heading: Personal pronouns
pronouns.text: Use the second-person pronoun ( you ) whenever possible. For more information about second person, see Second person and first person .

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: There are several relative pronouns. This section concerns only three of them: that , which , and who .

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: That and which don't mean exactly the same thing, so don't substitute one for the other:

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: That introduces a restrictive clause. It isn't preceded by a comma. Recommended : The echidna that has a long snout is furry. This sentence describes a particular echidna, the one that has a long snout.

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: Which introduces a nonrestrictive clause and is preceded by a comma. Recommended : The echidna, which has a long snout, is furry. This sentence describes all echidnas, and mentions in passing that they all have long snouts.

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: For more information about restrictive and nonrestrictive clauses and whether to use that or which , read what Grammar Girl has to say on the subject .

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: When you're referring to a person, you can use who instead of that . If you're not sure which pronoun is appropriate in your context, then it's generally OK to use that .

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: You can use whose to refer to people, animals, and things. Whose is the possessive form of both who and which .

pronouns.heading: Relative pronouns
pronouns.text: Recommended : Examine the variables whose values are set at compile time.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: In general, address the reader of your documents using the second person instead of the first person: use you or your instead of we , our , or us . Assume that the reader is the person who's doing the tasks or making the decisions. Use the word user only to refer to the user of the software that your reader is developing.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: The following sections describe how you can create a website. The following sections describe how we can create a website.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: Consider adding a description to your table. Let's add a description to our table.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: This document shows you how to develop an app for your organization. This document shows the user how to develop an app for their organization.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: If you're telling the reader to do something, then use the imperative (the you is implied). For example:

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: It's OK to use the imperative in running text after you establish who is being addressed. However, consider whether the imperative text needs to be formatted as as a procedure.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: Recommended : You can obtain the IP address for the appliance from your network administrator. Store the address in a variable for future use in the runbook.

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: Not recommended : To hold the backup data, create a storage bucket. In the Google Cloud console, go to the Buckets page. Click Create bucket .

person.heading: Address the reader as you
person.text: There are some situations in which using you might not be accurate or appropriate. Use the second person to address what the reader does, but use the third person for what the software or an end user does. For example, in API documentation, you can use the third person when you state facts about programming elements, but address the reader as you when you tell them what to do with them.

person.heading: Use first-person plural pronouns carefully
person.text: It's OK to use first-person plural pronouns (such as we , our , or us ) to refer to the organization that's represented as the author of the document. However, ensure that the antecedent for the pronoun is clear.

person.heading: Use first-person plural pronouns carefully
person.text: Recommended : Example Organization provides A and B, but we don't provide C and D.

person.heading: Use first-person plural pronouns carefully
person.text: Recommended : For more information, contact our sales organization.

person.heading: Use first-person plural pronouns carefully
person.text: Recommended : The example.org support team regularly reviews tickets. Expect to hear from us in 2-3 business days.

person.heading: Address your audience consistently
person.text: It's important to identify who the you is that you're addressing (a developer? a sysadmin? someone else?) and to be consistent about that. Make it clear to the reader who you expect them to be (sometimes with an explicit audience sentence near the beginning of the document).

sentence-structure.text: If you want to tell the reader to do something, try to mention the circumstance, conditions, or goal before you provide the instruction. Mentioning the circumstance first lets the reader skip the instruction if it doesn't apply. For information about how to apply this guideline to procedural instructions, see Procedures .
For more information, see [link to other document]. See [link to other document] for more information.
To delete the entire document, click Delete . Click Delete if you want to delete the entire document.

reference-verbs.text: When you're writing reference documentation for a method, phrase the main method description in terms of what the method does ( gets , lists , creates , searches ), rather than what the developer would use it to do ( get , list , create , search ).
It's a subtle distinction that manifests mostly in whether the initial verb in the description has an -s at the end or not.
Recommended : tasks.insert: Creates a new task on the specified task list.
Not recommended : tasks.insert: Create a new task on the specified task list.

colons.text: In general, the first word in the text that follows a colon should be in lowercase. For exceptions, see Capitalization and colons .

commas.text: Use commas to separate items in a series, and use commas to separate certain kinds of clauses. Serial commas In a series of three or more items, use a comma before the final and or or to avoid potentially changing the meaning of the sentence. This comma is called a serial comma or an Oxford comma. Recommended : Locations are divided into zones, regions, and multi-regions. Not recommended : Locations are divided into zones, regions and multi-regions. Commas after introductory words and phrases In general, place a comma after an introductory word or phrase. Recommended : Finally, only groups that contain parameters appear in this list. Recommended : Based on the requirements of your game, you can implement this method to update game information. Commas separating two independent clauses When a coordinating conjunction ( and , but , or , nor , for , so , or yet ) separates two independent clauses, insert a comma after the first clause (before the conjunction) unless both clauses are very short. Recommended : The libraries make feed creation easier, and they ensure that only valid feeds are produced. Not recommended : The libraries make feed creation easier and they ensure that only valid feeds are produced. Recommended : Type your ID and click OK . Not recommended : Type your ID, and click OK . Commas separating independent from dependent clauses When an independent clause and a dependent clause are separated by a coordinating conjunction, insert a comma only if the sentence could be misunderstood without one. Recommended : Direct-access flags are plain variables and can be read directly. Not recommended : Direct-access flags are plain variables, and can be read directly. Recommended : The manager acknowledged the last team member who entered the room, and started the meeting. Not recommended : The manager acknowledged the last team member who entered the room and started the meeting. Set off other kinds of clauses It's often a good idea to set off certain kinds of clauses with a comma or other punctuation for clarity. A couple of specific places where commas are a good idea: In general, put a comma before the word which at the start of a nonrestrictive clause. For more information about this topic, see this guide's section on relative pronouns and Grammar Girl's page on which versus that . In general, put a semicolon or a period or a dash before a conjunctive adverb, such as otherwise , however , or therefore , and put a comma after the conjunctive adverb. In general, don't use a comma before the causal conjunction because unless it starts a nonrestrictive clause. For more information, see the Chicago Manual of Style Q&A entry on using commas with because . Recommended Not recommended Name of the group, which has a maximum length of 200 characters. Name of the group which has a maximum length of 200 characters. The variable must have a value; otherwise, the server returns an error. The variable must have a value otherwise the server returns an error. You can use the same key name in multiple backend services and backend buckets, because each set of keys is independent of the others. You can use the same key name in multiple backend services and backend buckets because each set of keys is independent of the others. dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: To indicate a break in the flow of a sentence—or an interruption—use an em dash, also known as a long dash. Don't put a space before or after it.

dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: You can type the em dash character in various ways:

dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: HTML: —

dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: macOS: Press Option+Shift+hyphen .

dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: Linux desktop environment: Enable the Compose key (instructions for doing that vary depending on your flavor of Linux—for examples, see Linux Keyboard Shortcuts For Text Symbols ). After the Compose key is enabled, you can create an em dash by typing the Compose key followed by three hyphens. Alternatively, press Control+Shift+U . Let go of those keys, and then type 2014 . Then press Return . Note : These Linux options don't work if you're signed in to the Linux command line from a remote system using ssh or the like; you have to be in a Linux desktop environment.

dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: Windows: Turn num lock on, and then hold down the left Alt key and type 0151 on the numeric keypad.

dashes.heading: Em dashes
dashes.text: Don't use an en dash (the shorter dash) or a hyphen in place of an em dash. The use of an en dash with spaces around it in place of an em dash is gradually becoming more common, but it's still not very widespread in the US in professional publishing; so far (as of early 2016), it's mostly used in Canada and a few other places. For now, only use the em dash.

dashes.heading: En dashes
dashes.text: Don't use. Instead, use a hyphen or the word to . For more information, see the following:

dashes.heading: En dashes
dashes.text: Ranges of numbers with units

dashes.heading: En dashes

dashes.heading: Colons instead of dashes in description lists
dashes.text: Another common but nonstandard construction is to use an em dash, an en dash, or a hyphen surrounded by spaces to separate an item and its description. Instead, use a colon or a period . For a series of items, use an HTML description list ( <dl> ).

dashes.heading: Colons instead of dashes in description lists
dashes.text: Recommended : Example: This is an example.

dashes.heading: Colons instead of dashes in description lists
dashes.text: Not recommended : Example - This is an example.

dashes.heading: Colons instead of dashes in description lists

dashes.heading: Colons instead of dashes in description lists
dashes.text: Not recommended : Appendix A—My first appendix

dashes.text: Recommended :

dashes.heading: Colons instead of dashes in description lists

ellipses.text: In general, don't use ellipses. An ellipsis is made up of three contiguous periods. Ellipses indicate the omission of part of a sentence, paragraph, or larger block of text where the omission is not pertinent to the understanding of the subject at hand.

ellipses.heading: Ellipses as suspension points
ellipses.text: When ellipses are used to indicate hesitation, they are called suspension points . Don't use ellipses this way in our documentation.

ellipses.heading: Ellipses as suspension points
ellipses.text: Not recommended : The answer is ... wait for it ... that you shouldn't do this.

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in a user interface
ellipses.text: When ellipses appear in a user interface, exclude them from the documentation describing the user interface unless their omission could cause confusion. For example, if the text on the button in the UI reads Save ... , document it as click Save .

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in text
ellipses.text: Don't use ellipses in your written documentation; omit any unnecessary information and include all necessary information.

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in text
ellipses.text: However, it's acceptable to use ellipses in quoted text (to replace a portion of the quoted text) except when they appear at the beginning or end of the text.

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in text
ellipses.text: Not recommended : My high school English teacher made me learn that Shakespeare quote about all the world being a stage and " ... all the men and women merely players."

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in text
ellipses.text: Not recommended : My high school English teacher made me learn that Shakespeare quote: "All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players ...."

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in text
ellipses.text: The previous example ended with four ellipsis points. The final ellipsis point is, in fact, a period. So when the material that you're omitting contains one or more sentence boundaries, use four dots instead of three.

ellipses.heading: Ellipses in text
ellipses.text: Recommended : My high school English teacher made me learn that Shakespeare quote: "All the world's a stage, .... And one man in his time plays many parts."

ellipses.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
ellipses.text: Keep all three ellipsis points together. When creating an ellipsis, instead of the ellipsis character, use three periods in a row. Insert one space before and after the ellipsis unless a punctuation mark immediately follows the ellipsis; in this case, don't insert a space after the ellipsis.

ellipses.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
ellipses.text: Recommended : You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there ... we'll explain it all in class.

ellipses.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
ellipses.text: Also recommended : You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there ...; we'll explain it all in class.

ellipses.heading: Punctuation and spacing of ellipses
ellipses.text: Not recommended : You don't need to understand all the other Python code in there...we'll explain it all in class.

hyphens.text: Use a hyphen (-) when needed for clarity. A hyphen can separate parts of words to avoid misreadings, and it can combine terms when they should be read as a unit.

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: Guidance for hyphenation isn't always straightforward because it depends on the following circumstances:

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: Location . For example, does a term precede a noun, or does it follow a verb?

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: Interpretation and readability . Is a sentence ambiguous or unclear if a term is not hyphenated?

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: Convention . For some terms, our guidance tells us to always hyphenate or never hyphenate, even if the convention seems to contradict other guidance.

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: In addition, there are many exceptions to general hyphenation guidance. If you're not sure whether to hyphenate a term, in addition to reviewing the guidelines on this page, check the following sources (in this order):

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: The documentation that you're working with. If there's an established convention for hyphenating a term in a particular documentation set, follow that convention.

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: The word list in this style guide.

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: The Merriam-Webster dictionary .

hyphens.heading: General guidelines
hyphens.text: As always, deviate from our guidance when it serves your readers. For more information, see Break the rules .

hyphens.heading: Prefixes
hyphens.text: In general, don't use a hyphen between a prefix and the main noun.

hyphens.heading: Prefixes
hyphens.text: Recommended : infrastructure , megabyte , metadata , preprocessing , pseudocode , semiconductor

hyphens.heading: Exceptions
hyphens.text: Add a hyphen after a prefix in the following circumstances:

hyphens.heading: Exceptions
hyphens.text: If the prefix is self or cross : self-managing , cross-region

hyphens.heading: Exceptions
hyphens.text: If the noun is capitalized or is a number: non-Google , post-2000

hyphens.heading: Exceptions
hyphens.text: To avoid confusion or difficulty in reading: de-energize , intra-index , re-mark , re-sign

hyphens.heading: Exceptions
hyphens.text: If the prefix is for a term that already has hyphens or spaces: un-Google-like , non-twentieth-century

hyphens.heading: Exceptions
hyphens.text: To be consistent within a document: pre-processing , post-processing

hyphens.heading: The non prefix
hyphens.text: The non prefix follows the same guidelines, but because it can easily form words that are hard to parse, it's often hyphenated. Use your best judgment, taking into account consistency within your documentation. The following recommendations show contrasting usages that you can use as examples. Recommended : noncurrent , nonempty , noninteractive , nonpublic Recommended : non-existence , non-integer , non-key , non-managed , non-negative When using non as a prefix, add a hyphen before hyphenated compound words. Recommended : non-KSA-based , non-self-sustaining Compounds A compound is a term that combines more than one word. Compounds can be closed as one word with no spaces, open with spaces between words, or hyphenated. Compound nouns In general, write compound nouns in their closed (one-word, unhyphenated) form. If you see that Merriam-Webster.com uses the two-word or hyphenated form, but you see that the closed form is the predominant convention in your context or trending in that direction (as compounds often do), then use the closed form. Recommended : webpage Recommended : hostname Recommended : tradeoff Recommended : workaround Exceptions Our word list includes exceptions for well-established terms that commonly use a hyphen or a space, such as multi-region and style sheet . In some cases, we note that noun, verb, and adjective versions of a word are treated differently. When the components of a unit of measurement are multiplied by each other, hyphenate them. This guideline can be subjective. However, except as noted in this section, it's almost never wrong to hyphenate a compound before a noun to ensure clarity. Recommended : The goal is to produce an experience that's game-like. Range of numbers Use a hyphen, not an en dash ( – ), to indicate a range of numbers. If a hyphen introduces ambiguity, use words such as from , to , and through for clarity. Don't mix hyphens with words. For information about how to represent a range of numbers that includes units, see Ranges of numbers with units . Suspended hyphens When two or more compound modifiers have a common base, you can keep the hyphens but leave out the base for all except the last modifier. parentheses.text: Some of us love to use parentheses. Unfortunately, some readers ignore anything that appears in parentheses, so don't put important information in parentheses if you can help it.

Even for less important information, whenever you're inclined to use parentheses, consider whether they're necessary. Sometimes they are; however, the sentence or paragraph might work just as well if you remove the parentheses and set off the phrase or sentence by using commas, dashes, semicolons, or periods.
If you need to include parentheses in the middle of a sentence, keep the parenthetical thought short. Otherwise, consider using two sentences.

periods.text: End a complete sentence with a period, unless it's a question. There are exceptions for working in lists.

periods.heading: Periods with lists
periods.text: Whether to end a list item with a period depends on several factors, including the kind of list that the item appears in.

periods.heading: Periods with lists
periods.text: For details about how to use periods in lists, see the Capitalization and end punctuation section of the "Lists" page.

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: When a period immediately follows a URL or a file path, it can be hard to tell whether the period is part of the URL.

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: To indicate that the punctuating period isn't part of the URL, try one of the following techniques:

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: Whenever possible, avoid putting URLs in text .

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: Rewrite the sentence so that the URL isn't at the end of the sentence.

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: Put the URL on a separate line from the text, omitting the final period.

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: If the URL is a link, it generally looks different from the surrounding text. For example, in most browsers, link text is blue by default. This formatting helps distinguish the URL from the period.

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: Recommended :

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: We use your feedback to improve the Animals API, in accordance with Example Pet Store's Privacy Policy:

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: http://www.examplepetstore.com/privacy/

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: Not recommended :

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: We use your feedback to improve the Animals API, in accordance with Example Pet Store's Privacy Policy at http://www.examplepetstore.com/privacy/.

periods.heading: Periods with URLs
periods.text: When you do put a period after a URL, don't leave any space between the last character of the URL and the period.

periods.heading: Periods with quotation marks
periods.text: When a sentence ends with material inside quotation marks, place the period inside the quotation marks even if the period isn't part of the material inside the quotation marks. An exception to this guideline applies if you're using quotation marks around a keyword or other literal string. For more information, see Commas and periods with quotation marks .

periods.heading: Periods with quotation marks
periods.text: Recommended : ... you might say "Fixed typo."

periods.heading: Periods with quotation marks
periods.text: If the material inside the quotation marks ends with a question mark or an exclamation point, don't use a period.

periods.heading: Periods with quotation marks
periods.text: Recommended : Children always ask "Why?"

periods.heading: Periods with parentheses
periods.text: If the last part of a sentence is contained inside parentheses, put the period after the closing parenthesis.

periods.heading: Periods with parentheses
periods.text: If the parentheses contain a complete sentence, put the period inside the parentheses.

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: In general, avoid exclamation points. They can appear unprofessional, alarming, or translate poorly into other languages. If you need to use an exclamation point, see the following guidance by content type:

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: Concept and reference docs. Never use exclamation points. These sections should maintain a neutral, objective tone.

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: Procedural topics. Avoid exclamation points. Use periods for completion steps—for example, "The VM is created."

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: Blog posts. Exclamation points are acceptable to convey enthusiasm but shouldn't be used in every paragraph.

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: When exclamation points are acceptable:

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: Code examples. Use when required by syntax—for example, the != operator.

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: System literals. Use when an exclamation point is part of a specific error code or log message that must be matched exactly.

periods.heading: Exclamation points
periods.text: Tutorials and learning modules. Use sparingly to mark major milestones or achievements—for example, "Congratulations! You've completed the setup."

quotation-marks.text: Use straight double quotation marks and apostrophes.

quotation-marks.heading: When to use quotation marks
quotation-marks.text: In technical writing, we don't use quotation marks much, aside from instances of code.

quotation-marks.heading: When to use quotation marks
quotation-marks.text: Generally, you can use quotation marks for titles of shorter works such as articles or episodes in a web series, unless they're part of a link. For more information, see cross-references .

quotation-marks.heading: When to use quotation marks
quotation-marks.text: For most titles that are full-length works, we use italics.

quotation-marks.heading: When to use quotation marks
quotation-marks.text: For examples of when to use quotation marks in regular text, see the following table: Guidance Example Referring to a section of a larger document or piece, if you can't link to the section directly. The technique is described in the section "Deploying containers" of the Containers overview video. Referring to the title of a parent document when you're already linking to a section The machine learning (ML) workflow section of "Introduction to Vertex AI" describes the machine learning workflow for Vertex AI. Directly citing a person or quoting a slogan or motto. Martin Fowler has said, "We are still learning the techniques to write software effectively." Using a term metaphorically, but only if it's not an established usage in the domain. This configuration forms an "island" within the network that is not connected to the external network. For more information, see Text-formatting summary . Commas and periods with quotation marks Commas and periods go inside quotation marks. Recommended : See the section titled "Care and feeding of the emu." Not recommended : See the section titled "Care and feeding of the emu". Exception : When you put a keyword or other literal string in quotation marks, put any other punctuation outside the quotation marks. In those cases, the quotation marks indicate an exact literal string, so don't add anything extraneous inside the quotation marks. However, in general, don't put quotation marks around an item that's in code font, unless the quotation marks are part of the item. Recommended : If you enter escape , the program crashes. Acceptable : If you enter "escape", the program crashes. Not recommended : If you enter "escape," the program crashes. Straight and curly quotation marks Most typefaces support two forms of quotation marks and apostrophes: straight marks and curly, or typographic, marks. Some tools, like Google Docs, automatically convert straight quotation marks and apostrophes to the curly versions as you type. However, our guidance is to always use straight quotation marks and straight apostrophes in developer documentation, for the following reasons: It makes writing documents easier. Code requires straight marks, so it's simpler to use straight marks everywhere in developer documentation than to use them in code but not in text. Tools that automatically change straight marks to curly marks (such as word processors) often make mistakes. Humans who manually type curly marks also often make mistakes. Manually typing curly marks can be difficult on some platforms. It makes reviewing documents easier. When you're proofreading a document, it can be hard to see whether marks are straight or curly, and which direction they point in. In the following examples, the first example uses straight quotation marks and the second example uses curly quotation marks: Recommended : The section's title is "Care and feeding of the emu." Not recommended : The section’s title is “Care and feeding of the emu.” Single quotation marks The only times to use single quotation marks in our documentation are the following: In code examples, in languages that use single quotation marks. When nesting a quotation inside another quotation. In the latter case, put the primary speaker's quote in double quotation marks and the quote inside the primary speaker's quote in single quotation marks. Recommended : She said, "I heard him shout 'Help,' and saw him floundering in the water." Not recommended : She said, 'I heard him shout "Help", and saw him floundering in the water'. Note : For information about how to use quotation marks with links, see Quotation marks and italics .
