tables.heading: Introductory sentences for tables
tables.text: Introduce tables with a complete sentence that describes the purpose of the table because not all screen readers preannounce tables. The introductory sentence can end with a colon or a period; usually a colon if it immediately precedes the table, and usually a period if there's more material (such as a note paragraph) between the introduction and the table.

tables.heading: Introductory sentences for tables
tables.text: Recommended : Change the environment variables to values for your deployment, as listed in the following table:

tables.heading: Introductory sentences for tables
tables.text: For more information, see the Tables section of the "Accessibility" page.

tables.heading: Table placement
tables.text: When introducing a table, use a complete sentence and try to refer to the table's position, using a phrase like the following table or the preceding table .

tables.heading: Table placement
tables.text: Don't put a table in the middle of a sentence.

tables.heading: Table placement
tables.text: Avoid using footnotes when possible. If your table does refer to footnotes, place them immediately following the table. For more information, see Footnotes .

tables.heading: Table captions
tables.text: If your document contains only one table, the table doesn't need a caption. However, be sure to place the table adjacent to the text that refers to it.

tables.heading: Table captions
tables.text: If your document contains more than one table in fairly close proximity to each other, include a caption for each one, using a caption element as the first child of the table element. Start the caption with a number, in the form "Table NUMBER . DESCRIPTION ". Use sentence case for the caption, but don't place a period at the end.

tables.heading: Table captions
tables.text: When referring to the table from text, refer to it by its number—for example, ... as shown in table 2 . Do not capitalize table unless it starts a sentence.

tables.heading: Table captions
tables.text: Your site's CSS determines the styling and placement of the caption.

tables.heading: Table captions
tables.text: Recommended :

tables.heading: Table captions
tables.text:
...
Table 1. Prehistoric birds

tables.heading: Table formatting
tables.text: Don't add styling to the table element.

tables.heading: Table formatting
tables.text: Don't apply a visual style such as a different font, font color, or background color to convey a header row or column by itself. Use the th element to semantically mark up headers in tables.

tables.heading: Table formatting
tables.text: Don't merge cells. Don't use colspan or rowspan attributes.

tables.heading: Table formatting
tables.text: Sort rows in a logical order, or alphabetically if there is no logical order.

tables.heading: Table formatting
tables.text: If the table is long or complicated—for example, with multiple header rows or columns—consider splitting it into multiple tables.

tables.heading: Table formatting
tables.text: Don't present new information in tables through images or symbols alone; always provide a descriptive alt attribute for the image or symbol. For more information, see Alt text .

tables.heading: Table column heads
tables.text: Use sentence case.

tables.heading: Table column heads
tables.text: Write concise headings.

tables.heading: Table column heads
tables.text: Don't end with punctuation, including a period, an ellipsis, or a colon.

tables.heading: Table column heads
tables.text: Use table headings for the first column and the first row only. Use the th element .

tables.heading: Table column heads
tables.text: Include the scope attribute as appropriate for accessibility.

tables.heading: Responsive tables
tables.text: Where possible, use table CSS that adapts to different viewport sizes.

tables.heading: Link to tables
tables.text: Where possible, avoid linking to tables; instead, refer to them by table number.

units-of-measure.text: Put a nonbreaking space (   ) between the number and the unit.

units-of-measure.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
units-of-measure.text: For most units of measurement, when you specify a number with the unit, use a nonbreaking space between the number and the unit. This guidance applies in both HTML and Markdown.

units-of-measure.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
units-of-measure.text: For guidance about when to spell out units, see the Abbreviations page.

units-of-measure.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
units-of-measure.text: For guidance about whether to hyphenate, see the Hyphens page.

units-of-measure.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
units-of-measure.text: For more information about making abbreviations plural, see Plural abbreviations .

units-of-measure.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
units-of-measure.text: However, when the unit of measure is money or percent or degrees of an angle, don't use a space. For more information, see Currency .

units-of-measure.heading: Spaces in units of measurement
units-of-measure.text: For degrees of temperature, include a nonbreaking space between the number and the degree symbol. Don't use a space between the degree symbol ( ° ) and the temperature scale ( F or C ).

units-of-measure.heading: Markdown
units-of-measure.text: For Kelvin temperatures, leave out the degree symbol but use a nonbreaking space before the K .

units-of-measure.heading: Markdown
units-of-measure.text: When a number and unit of measurement combine to modify a noun, don't hyphenate unless the hyphen is needed for clarity.

units-of-measure.heading: Ranges of numbers with units
units-of-measure.text: In a range of numbers, repeat the unit for each number. Unit includes both symbols (like the degree symbol (º)) and abbreviations (like MB for megabytes) but not nouns (like file ). For more information, see Range of numbers .

units-of-measure.heading: Ranges of numbers with units
units-of-measure.text: Use the word to between the numbers, rather than a hyphen. A hyphen can be misinterpreted as a subtraction sign.

units-of-measure.heading: Hyphens with multiplied units
units-of-measure.text: When the components of a unit of measurement are multiplied by each other, hyphenate them.

units-of-measure.heading: Use k to indicate thousands
units-of-measure.text: In some contexts, it might be appropriate to indicate thousands of something by following a number with a lowercase k . If you do that, then follow these guidelines:

units-of-measure.heading: Use k to indicate thousands
units-of-measure.text: Don't put a space between the number and k .

units-of-measure.heading: Use k to indicate thousands
units-of-measure.text: Add a noun to indicate what the number measures, and to make clear that you're not using k as an abbreviation for kilobytes .

units-of-measure.heading: Use k to indicate thousands
units-of-measure.text: Recommended : On this plan, you are limited to 55k download operations and 20k upload operations per day.

units-of-measure.heading: Currency
units-of-measure.text: If you're writing about monetary amounts, make sure that the reader knows what currency you're referring to. For example, the dollar sign—the $ symbol—can refer to US dollars, Canadian dollars, Mexican pesos, and several other currencies.

units-of-measure.heading: Currency
units-of-measure.text: If there's any possibility of ambiguity, use a currency indicator before the amount. For details, see section 9.20 and following in the Chicago Manual of Style , 17th edition.

units-of-measure.heading: Rates
units-of-measure.text: Use per instead of the division slash (/) when space permits. It's OK to use the division slash when space is limited, such as in a table with small cells.

units-of-measure.heading: Rates
units-of-measure.text: Shorten per to p only for well-established abbreviations for rate units, such as Gbps for gigabits per second or MBps for megabytes per second .

units-of-measure.heading: Decimal and binary units
units-of-measure.text: Use the same system to measure bytes as the technology that you're documenting. Don't use MB if you mean MiB , or GB if you mean GiB . The following table lists common types of decimal and binary units :

units-of-measure.heading: Decimal and binary units
units-of-measure.text: kB (kilobyte, or 1000 bytes) KiB (kibibyte, or 1024 bytes)

units-of-measure.heading: Decimal and binary units
units-of-measure.text: MB (megabyte, or 1000 2 bytes) MiB (mebibyte, or 1024 2 bytes)

units-of-measure.heading: Decimal and binary units
units-of-measure.text: GB (gigabyte, or 1000 3 bytes) GiB (gibibyte, or 1024 3 bytes)

units-of-measure.heading: Decimal and binary units
units-of-measure.text: For more information about abbreviating measurement terms, see When to spell out a term .

cross-references.text: In general, cross-references link to nonessential information that adds to the reader's understanding.

When used well, cross-references help readers navigate and understand documentation. But cross-references can easily become disruptive. The guidelines on this page help you to minimize disruption while providing cross-references that help your readers.

cross-references.heading: Choose links selectively
cross-references.text: Be selective about which links you include on a page. Each link creates a decision for the reader, adding cognitive load. Each link is also a chance for the reader to leave the page and lose their place. When you include links, choose the most relevant destination.

cross-references.heading: Provide context on the page
cross-references.text: When possible, provide help in context rather than linking elsewhere. For example, in the following situations, consider providing information on the page instead of linking:

cross-references.heading: Provide context on the page
cross-references.text: Define a term.

cross-references.heading: Provide context on the page
cross-references.text: Briefly explain a concept.

cross-references.heading: Provide context on the page
cross-references.text: Provide a couple of steps.

cross-references.heading: Provide context on the page
cross-references.text: As a specific example, if you need readers to understand another product's software or standards, it's better to link to good documentation elsewhere than to try to thoroughly document another product's standards in our documentation. But if a few sentences of basic information is all your readers need, then it's better to provide that context and save your readers the trip outside of our documentation.

cross-references.heading: Avoid duplicate links
cross-references.text: Generally, within a given page, don't provide duplicate links to the same destination. Provide the link once in the location where it's most useful to the reader.

cross-references.heading: Avoid duplicate links
cross-references.text: It's OK to add a secondary link in situations such as the following:

cross-references.heading: Avoid duplicate links
cross-references.text: You're linking to a particular section of another page.

cross-references.heading: Avoid duplicate links
cross-references.text: Your page is very long and the duplicate links are far apart.

cross-references.heading: Avoid duplicate links
cross-references.text: There are multiple entry points to the document that you're linking from. For example, if a page contains a procedure section and a troubleshooting section, then you might need to provide the same link in both of those sections.

cross-references.heading: Provide the most relevant link
cross-references.text: When you link, link to the most relevant page on a site. Link to the most relevant heading on a page. Avoid providing multiple links that do the same job.

cross-references.heading: Link to third-party sites
cross-references.text: Our documentation often relies on the reader knowing something about third-party standards or software. In such cases, it's better to provide a link rather than attempt to thoroughly document someone else's standards. But as with all links, when possible, provide brief information on the page instead of linking.

cross-references.heading: Write descriptive link text
cross-references.text: For the link text itself, use short, unique, descriptive phrases that provide context for the material that you're linking to.

cross-references.heading: Write descriptive link text
cross-references.text: Effective link text helps to improve accessibility and scannability. Different readers experience links differently. For example, users of screen reader software often jump from one link to the next without reading the words in between. Other readers visually scan a document to find relevant links.

cross-references.heading: Write descriptive link text
cross-references.text: Sometimes you have to rework a sentence to include a phrase that makes good link text.

cross-references.heading: Two options for effective link text
cross-references.text: For your link text, use either the exact page title or a descriptive phrase, as described in the following sections.

cross-references.heading: Page titles as link text
cross-references.text: One option for effective link text is to match the link text to the page title or heading that you're referencing.

cross-references.heading: Page titles as link text
cross-references.text: For more information about how to capitalize the page title in a cross-reference, see Capitalization in references to titles and headings .

cross-references.heading: Page titles as link text
cross-references.text: Recommended : For more information, see Load balancing and scaling .

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: Another option for effective link text is to use a description of the destination page, capitalized as if it's part of the sentence.

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: When you write a descriptive phrase as link text, help readers quickly determine whether the link is relevant to them:

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: Place important words at the beginning of the link text.

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: Don't use the same link text in the same document for different target pages.

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: Keep link text short where possible. Don't write lengthy link text such as a sentence or short paragraph.

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: Recommended : You can use Cloud Scheduler and Cloud Functions to manage task scheduling on Compute Engine .

cross-references.heading: Descriptive phrases as link text
cross-references.text: Not recommended : See this blog post .

cross-references.heading: Avoid vague link text
cross-references.text: Write link text that makes sense without the surrounding text. Don't use phrases such as this document , this article , or click here .

cross-references.heading: Avoid vague link text
cross-references.text: Recommended : For more information, see Make headings into link targets .

cross-references.heading: Avoid vague link text
cross-references.text: Not recommended : Want more? Click here!

cross-references.heading: Avoid vague link text
cross-references.text: Not recommended : For more information, see this document .

cross-references.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
cross-references.text: In general, don't use a URL as link text. Instead, use the page title or a description of the page.

cross-references.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
cross-references.text: Recommended :

cross-references.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
cross-references.text: For more information about protocols, see HTTP/1.1 RFC.

cross-references.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
cross-references.text: Not recommended :

cross-references.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
cross-references.text: See the HTTP/1.1 RFC at http://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616.html.

cross-references.heading: Avoid URLs as link text
cross-references.text: Exception : In some legal documents (such as some Terms of Service documents), it's okay to use URLs as link text.

cross-references.heading: Include abbreviations in link text
cross-references.text: If the text includes an abbreviation in parentheses, include the long form and the abbreviation in the link text.

cross-references.heading: Include abbreviations in link text
cross-references.text: Recommended : Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)

cross-references.heading: Include abbreviations in link text
cross-references.text: Not recommended : Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)

cross-references.heading: Link to commands
cross-references.text: If the text includes a command or another element usually conveyed with code font, include the description of the code element with the link text, unless doing so is awkward or redundant. For more information about elements that appear in code font, see Code in text .

cross-references.heading: Link to commands
cross-references.text: Recommended : To create an instance with a custom hostname, run the gcloud instances create command with the --hostname flag .

cross-references.heading: Link to commands
cross-references.text: Not recommended : To create an instance with a custom hostname, run the gcloud instances create command with the --hostname flag.

cross-references.heading: Link to commands
cross-references.text: Recommended : This service supports the GET , HEAD , and OPTIONS methods.

cross-references.heading: Link to commands
cross-references.text: Not recommended : This service supports the GET method , HEAD method , and OPTIONS method .

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: When you dedicate a separate sentence to a cross-reference, introduce the cross-reference using consistent language—specifically, use the phrase "For more information, see..." or "For more information about..., see... ."

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: Include the "about..." clause when the link text or surrounding context doesn't clearly indicate why you're referring the reader to this information. For more information, see the Clarify the purpose of a link section of this document.

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: Don't use on instead of about .

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: Use see to refer to links and cross-references. For more information, see see .

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: Recommended : For more information, see Load balancing and scaling .

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: Recommended : For more information about task scheduling, see Reliable task scheduling on Google Compute Engine .

cross-references.heading: Write link introductions ("For more information")
cross-references.text: Not recommended : For more information on indexes, see Manage indexes .

cross-references.heading: Clarify the purpose of a link
cross-references.text: Make sure that the surrounding context or the link text itself clearly indicates why you're referring the reader to this information. Make the explanation specific, but don't repeat the link text.

cross-references.heading: Clarify the purpose of a link
cross-references.text: If you're introducing a cross-reference with "For more information..." phrasing, then you can do this by adding an "about..." phrase. For more information, see the Write link introductions section of this document.

cross-references.heading: Clarify the purpose of a link
cross-references.text: Recommended : For more information about authentication and authorization, see Using OAuth 2.0 to access Google APIs .

cross-references.heading: Clarify the purpose of a link
cross-references.text: Recommended : If your sample dump file is in a CSV, Avro, or Parquet file format, then load the file to BigQuery and copy to Spanner using reverse ETL.

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: If a link goes to an unexpected destination or behaves in an unexpected way, then provide that context. The following are a few such situations:

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: Links that download files and open emails. If a link downloads a file or opens an email, then make that clear in the link text, and mention the file type. Recommended : For more information, download the security features PDF . Recommended : send email to Technical Support

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: send email to Technical Support

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: Links to sections on the same page. When you're linking to another section on the same page, let the reader know that the link takes you to a different section of the same page. Use a standard phrase to clue readers in if you use an on-page link.

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: Links to sections on another page. When you're linking to a section heading on another page, use the same wording and formatting as you do in a regular cross-reference. If the title of the section that you're linking to is identical to a title on the source page, add context to the cross-reference. Recommended : For more information, see Create a table . Recommended : For more information, see Install libraries in "Building new audiences based on existing customer lifetime value."

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: Links that open in a new tab. For more information, see the Open links in the current tab section of this document.

cross-references.heading: Explain unexpected link behavior
cross-references.text: Links that go to a different domain or server. For more information, see the Don't use external link icons section of this document.

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: Don't force links to open in a new tab or window. Let the reader decide how to open links.

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: In the rare situation that a link needs to open in a new tab or window, let the reader know that the link opens differently than expected.

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: Recommended :

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: Accessible content

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: Recommended :

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: Accessible content (opens in a new tab)

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab
cross-references.text: Not recommended :

cross-references.heading: Open links in the current tab

headings-targets.text: This page discusses how to turn a heading into a link target by using an id attribute. For more information about how to format headings, see Headings and titles .
In some content management systems, anchors are automatically created for headings. However, you might want to add a custom anchor to a heading for several reasons:
You want to use an anchor that's shorter than the automatically generated anchor.
You want to use an anchor for content that might be frequently linked to. Adding a custom anchor reduces the likelihood of breaking existing links if the heading text changes later.
You want to revise a heading . If the anchor for the heading is generated automatically, then the anchor changes when you revise the heading, breaking existing links.

Add a custom anchor HTML To add an anchor to a heading in HTML, add a section element with an id attribute, or use an a element with a name attribute. For anchor text, use lowercase letters, and put hyphens between words. In the following, replace ID_OF_ANCHOR with your anchor text—for example, introduction-to-everything .
Recommended :

Introduction to everything

...
Recommended :

Introduction to everything

Recommended :

Introduction to everything

Acceptable :

Introduction to everything

Markdown To add an anchor to a heading in Markdown, add the following code to the end of the line that the heading is on. For anchor text, use lowercase letters, and put hyphens between words. In the following, replace ID_OF_ANCHOR with your anchor text—for example, conserve-habitat . {: # ID_OF_ANCHOR } Recommended : ## Help conserve habitat for pollinators {: #help-conserve-habitat-for-pollinators } Also recommended : ## Help conserve habitat for pollinators {: #conserve-habitat } Acceptable : ## Help conserve habitat for pollinators {: id='conserve-habitat' } Acceptable : ## Help conserve habitat for pollinators {: id="conserve-habitat" } Revise a heading If you revise a heading in a content management system where anchors are automatically created, you can create a custom anchor to avoid breaking existing links. If the heading already has a custom anchor, don't change the anchor unless it contains a term that you want to remove (such as a disrespectful term). To create the custom anchor, use the older ID string for the heading. You can find the ID string by inspecting the heading on the published page. For example, if you change a heading from Introduction to some things to Introduction to everything , then add a custom anchor that uses the older ID string and formatting. HTML

Introduction to everything

...
Markdown ## Introduction to everything {: #introduction-to-some-things } If you need to change an existing custom anchor, you should check your content management system to update any links that use the old anchor. Inbound links that use the old anchor still reach the page but not the specific section or heading.

headings-targets.heading: HTML
headings-targets.text: To add an anchor to a heading in HTML, add a section element with an id attribute, or use an a element with a name attribute. For anchor text, use lowercase letters, and put hyphens between words. In the following, replace ID_OF_ANCHOR with your anchor text—for example, introduction-to-everything .

headings-targets.heading: Markdown
headings-targets.text: To add an anchor to a heading in Markdown, add the following code to the end of the line that the heading is on. For anchor text, use lowercase letters, and put hyphens between words. In the following, replace ID_OF_ANCHOR with your anchor text—for example, conserve-habitat .

headings-targets.heading: Markdown
headings-targets.text: ## Help conserve habitat for pollinators {: id='conserve-habitat' }

headings-targets.heading: Markdown
headings-targets.text: ## Help conserve habitat for pollinators {: id="conserve-habitat" }

headings-targets.heading: Revise a heading
headings-targets.text: If you revise a heading in a content management system where anchors are automatically created, you can create a custom anchor to avoid breaking existing links. If the heading already has a custom anchor, don't change the anchor unless it contains a term that you want to remove (such as a disrespectful term).

headings-targets.heading: Revise a heading
headings-targets.text: To create the custom anchor, use the older ID string for the heading. You can find the ID string by inspecting the heading on the published page. For example, if you change a heading from Introduction to some things to Introduction to everything , then add a custom anchor that uses the older ID string and formatting.

headings-targets.text: If you need to change an existing custom anchor, you should check your content management system to update any links that use the old anchor. Inbound links that use the old anchor still reach the page but not the specific section or heading.

api-reference-comments.text: When you're documenting an API, provide a complete API reference, typically generated from source code using document comments that describe all public classes, methods, constants, and other members.
Use the basic guidelines in this document as appropriate for a given programming language. This document doesn't specify how to mark up document comments.
For more information, see the following resources:
AIP-192: Documentation in Google's API standards
Inline API documentation in the Google Cloud API design guide
The specific style guide for each programming language

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: The API reference must provide a description for each of the following:

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Every class, interface, struct, and any other similar member of the API (such as union types in C++).

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Every constant, field, enum, and typedef.

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Every method, with a description for each parameter, the return value, and any exceptions thrown.

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: The following are extremely strong suggestions . In some cases, they don't make sense for a particular API or in a specific language, but in general, follow these guidelines:

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: On each unique page (for a class, interface, etc.), include a code sample (~5-20 lines) at the top.

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Put all API names, classes, methods, constants, and parameters in code font, and link each name to the corresponding reference page. Most document generators do this automatically for you.

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Put string literals in code font, and enclose them in double quotation marks. For example, XML attribute values might be "wrap_content" or "true" .

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Make sure that the spelling of a class name in documentation matches the spelling in code, with capital letters and no spaces (for example, ActionBar ).

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: Don't make class names plural ( Intents , Activities ); instead, add a plural noun ( Intent objects, Activity instances). For more information, see Plural product and feature names .

api-reference-comments.heading: Documentation basics
api-reference-comments.text: However, if a class has a name that's a common term, you can refer to it with the corresponding English word, in lowercase and not in code font (activities, action bar).

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: In the first sentence of a class description, briefly state the intended purpose or function of the class or interface with information that can't be deduced from the class name and signature. In additional documentation, elaborate on how to use the API, including how to invoke or instantiate it, what some of the key features are, and any best practices or pitfalls.

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: Many documentation tools automatically extract the first sentence of each class description for use in a list of all classes, so make the first sentence unique and descriptive, yet short. Additionally:

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: Don't repeat the class name in the first sentence.

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: Don't say "this class will/does ..."

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: Don't use a period before the actual end of the sentence, because some document generators naively terminate the "short description" at the first period. For example, some generators terminate the sentence if they see e.g. , so use for example instead.

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: The following example is the first sentence of the description for Android's ActionBar class :

api-reference-comments.heading: Classes, interfaces, structs
api-reference-comments.text: A primary toolbar within the activity that may display the activity title, application-level navigation affordances, and other interactive items.

api-reference-comments.heading: Members
api-reference-comments.text: Make descriptions for members (constants and fields) as brief as possible. Be sure to link to relevant methods that use the constant or field.

api-reference-comments.heading: Members
api-reference-comments.text: For example, here's the description for the ActionBar class's DISPLAY_SHOW_HOME constant:

api-reference-comments.heading: Members
api-reference-comments.text: Show 'home' elements in this action bar, leaving more space for other navigation elements. This includes logo and icon.

api-reference-comments.heading: Members
api-reference-comments.text: See also: setDisplayOptions(int) , setDisplayOptions(int, int)

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: In the first sentence for a method description, briefly state what action the method performs. In subsequent sentences, explain why and how to use the method, state any prerequisites that must be met before calling it, give details about exceptions that may occur, and specify any related APIs.

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: Document any dependencies (such as Android permissions ) that are needed to call the method, and how the method behaves if such a dependency is missing (for example, "the method throws a SecurityException " or "the method returns null").

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: For example, here's the description for Android's Activity.isChangingConfigurations method :

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: Checks whether this activity is in the process of being destroyed in order to be recreated with a new configuration. This is often used in onStop to determine whether the state needs to be cleaned up or if it's passed on to the next instance of the activity using onRetainNonConfigurationInstance .

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: Use present tense for all descriptions—for example:

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: Adds a new bird to the ornithology list.

api-reference-comments.heading: Methods
api-reference-comments.text: Returns a bird.

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: If a method performs an operation and returns some data, start the description with a verb describing the operation—for example:

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: Adds a new bird to the ornithology list and returns the ID of the new entry.

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: If it's a "getter" method and it returns a boolean, start with "Checks whether ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: If it's a "getter" method and it returns something other than a boolean, start with "Gets the ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: If it has no return value, start with a verb like one of the following:

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: Turning on an ability or setting: "Sets the ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: Updating a property: "Updates the ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: Deleting something: "Deletes the ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: Registering a callback or other element for later reference: "Registers ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: For a callback: "Called by ...." (Usually for a method that's named starting with "on", such as onBufferingUpdate .) For example, "Called by Android when ...." Then, later in the description: "Subclasses implement this method to ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Description
api-reference-comments.text: If it's a convenience method that constructs the class object, start with "Creates a ...."

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: For parameter descriptions, follow these guidelines:

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: Capitalize the first word, and end the sentence or phrase with a period.

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: Begin descriptions of non-boolean parameters with "The" or "A" if possible:

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: The ID of the bird you want to get.

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: A description of the bird.

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: For boolean parameters that tell the API to do or not do something, state what the API does if the parameter is true and if it's false. For example:

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: enableCertificateValidation : If true, validates the SSL certificate before proceeding. If false, trusts the certificate without validating it.

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: For boolean parameters that declare the already-established state of something (rather than telling the API to do something), use the format "True if ...; false otherwise." For example:

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: True if the zoom is set; false otherwise.

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: In this context, don't put the words "true" and "false" in code font or quotation marks.

api-reference-comments.heading: Parameters
api-reference-comments.text: For parameters with default behavior, explain what the behavior is for each value or range of values, and then say what the default value is. Use the format Default: to explain the default value.

api-reference-comments.heading: Return values
api-reference-comments.text: Be as brief as possible in the return value's description; put any detailed information in the class description.

api-reference-comments.heading: Return values
api-reference-comments.text: If the return value is anything other than a boolean, start with "The ..."—for example:

api-reference-comments.heading: Return values
api-reference-comments.text: The bird specified by the given ID.

code-in-text.text: In ordinary text sentences (as opposed to, say, code samples ), use code font to mark up most things that have anything to do with code. Code font helps to clarify for your reader which text refers to an entity in these ways:
Signals to your reader that the text is meant to be entered verbatim.
Shows where the boundaries of the text to enter are.
Clearly separates the entity from surrounding text.
To mark text as code font, use the following:
In HTML, use the code element.
In Markdown, use backticks ( ` ).
For information about choosing HTML or Markdown, see Markdown versus HTML .

code-samples.text: This page explains how to format code samples. For more information about formatting and explaining code that appears in text, command-line syntax, and placeholders, see the following resources:
Code in text

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Follow these guidelines when formatting code samples:

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Follow the indentation guidelines in the relevant code style guide . For most programming languages, this means using spaces instead of tabs and using two spaces for each indentation level. However, some contexts use four spaces for each indentation level, and some contexts use tabs. This guidance applies to formatting code samples, not to formatting commands .

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Wrap lines at 80 characters. If you expect readers to have a relatively narrow browser window or to print out your document, consider wrapping at a smaller number of characters for readability.

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Mark code blocks as preformatted text . In HTML, use a pre element; in Markdown, indent every line of the code block by four spaces.

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Indicate omitted code by using a comment in the syntax of the language of your code sample. Don't use three dots or the ellipsis character ( … ). If a code block contains an omission, don't format the block as click-to-copy.

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Recommended :

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: function helloWorld() { alert('Hello, world! This sentence is so long that it wraps onto a second line.'); }

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: This renders the following code block:

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: function helloWorld() { alert('Hello, world! This sentence is so long that it wraps onto a second line.'); }

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: Recommended :

code-samples.heading: Basic guidelines
code-samples.text: apiVersion : serving.knative.dev/v1 kind : Service # Several lines of code are omitted here. spec : template : spec : containers : - image : IMAGE_URL ports : - name : h2c containerPort : 8080

code-samples.heading: Introductory statements
code-samples.text: In most cases, precede a code sample with an introductory sentence or paragraph. The introduction can end with a colon or a period; usually a colon if it immediately precedes the sample, usually a period if there's more material (such as a note paragraph) between the introduction and the sample, or if the introduction paragraph ends in a sentence that isn't directly related to the sample.

code-samples.heading: Introductory statements
code-samples.text: Recommended (ending with a period): The following code sample shows how to use the get method. For information about other methods, see [link]. [sample]

code-samples.heading: Introductory statements
code-samples.text: Also recommended : The following code sample shows how to use the get method: [sample] For information about other methods, see [link].

code-samples.heading: Introductory statements
code-samples.text: Not recommended (ending with a colon): The following code sample shows how to use the get method. For information about other methods, see [link]: [sample]

code-samples.heading: Introductory statements

code-syntax.text: This page shows how to document command-line commands and their arguments. For more information about formatting code that appears in text, placeholders, and code samples, see the following links:
Code in text
Formatting placeholders
Code samples

code-syntax.heading: Best practices
code-syntax.text: When you write procedural or conceptual documentation for a command-line command, apply the following best practices:

code-syntax.heading: Best practices
code-syntax.text: Provide an inline link to the command reference . A good place for that link is in the text that introduces the command or a series of steps. Recommended : To connect to the instance, use the gcloud compute ssh command : gcloud compute ssh

code-syntax.heading: Best practices
code-syntax.text: gcloud compute ssh

code-syntax.heading: Best practices
code-syntax.text: Determine which arguments are needed to complete each task in the recommended way . To minimize the number of options that you need to document in non-reference content, use as few optional arguments as possible. Rely on the command reference for the complete list of arguments.

code-syntax.heading: Best practices
code-syntax.text: Provide a click-to-copy command example that the reader doesn't need to edit after they copy it . If possible, include only runnable code and placeholder variables in the click-to-copy example. Some command examples contain optional arguments , mutually exclusive arguments , or repeated arguments that are indicated by square brackets ( [] ), pipes ( | ), braces ( {} ), and ellipses ( ... ). These characters can break commands if they're not first removed. For that reason, avoid using these arguments in click-to-copy examples. For more information, see the Optional arguments in click-to-copy commands section of this document.

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: To mark a block of code such as a lengthy command or a code sample, use the following formatting:

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: In HTML, use the pre element.

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: In Markdown, use a code fence ( ``` ).

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: To format a command with multiple elements, do the following:

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: When a line exceeds 80 characters, you can safely add a line break before some characters, such as a single hyphen, double hyphen, underscore, or quotation marks. After the first line, indent each line by four spaces to vertically align each line that follows a line break.

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: When you split a command line with a line break, each line except the last line must end with the command-continuation character. Commands that don't have the command-continuation character don't work.

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: Linux or Cloud Shell: A backslash typically preceded with a space ( \ )

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: Windows: A caret preceded with a space ( ^ )

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: Format placeholder text with placeholders .

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: Follow the command line with a descriptive list of the placeholders used in the command line. For more information, see Explaining placeholders .

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: When documenting a command-line option or argument, use end puctuation for complete sentences. Don't use end punctuation for single words or noun phrases, unless there is a mix of sentences and noun phrases. This guidance is similar to end punctuation in lists . For more information, see Google AIP guidelines for documentation .

code-syntax.heading: Format a command
code-syntax.text: When you're documenting a bash or sh command, follow the quotation mark style in Google's shell style guide.

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: If your command-line instructions show multiple lines of input in one block, then start each line of input with the prompt symbol. If you don't want users to copy the prompt symbol when they copy the command, you might be able to turn off text selection for the symbol—for example, by using CSS.

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: Don't show the current directory path before the prompt, even if part of the instruction includes changing directories. However, if the overall context of the command interface changes—such as from the local machine to a remote machine—then add an additional prompt indicator, as appropriate, for the new context.

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: Recommended :

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: Enter the following code into the terminal:

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: $ adb devices

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: The output is the following:

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: List of devices attached emulator-5554 device emulator-5556 device

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: Recommended :

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: $ adb shell shell@ $ screencap /sdcard/screen.png shell@ $ exit $ adb pull /sdcard/screen.png

code-syntax.heading: Command prompt
code-syntax.text: When you're showing a one-line command, the command prompt (the $ symbol) is optional. However, if your document includes both multi-line and one-line commands, then we recommend using the command prompt for all of the commands in the document for consistency.

Command-line terminology When discussing commands and their constituent parts in the gcloud CLI and in Linux commands, follow this guidance: Avoid mapping nomenclature of the gcloud CLI's commands to Linux commands. Linux commands can be complicated. It's wise to describe what the entire command does rather than what its individual elements are called. For Linux commands or commands in the gcloud CLI, ask yourself if the reader must know the name of the command-line element or if explaining the command is sufficient. gcloud commands gcloud GROUP | COMMAND [--account= ACCOUNT ] [--configuration= CONFIGURATION ] \ [--flatten=[ KEY ,...]][--format= FORMAT ] [--help] [--project= PROJECT_ID ] \ [--quiet, -q][--verbosity= VERBOSITY ; default="warning"] [--version, -v] \ [-h] [--log-http][--trace-token= TRACE_TOKEN ] [--no-user-output-enabled] For the sake of accurate classification, the gcloud CLI's syntax distinguishes between a command and a command group . In docs, however, command-line contents are generally referred to as commands. You can use commands (and groups) alone or with one or more flags. A flag is a Google Cloud-specific term for any element other than the command or group name itself. A command or flag might also take an argument , for example, a region value. Example command gcloud init Example command with a flag gcloud init --skip-diagnostics Example command with multiple elements gcloud ml-engine jobs submit training ${JOB_NAME} \ --package-path=trainer \ --module-name=trainer.task \ --staging-bucket=gs://${BUCKET} \ --job-dir=gs://${BUCKET}/${JOB_NAME} \ --runtime-version=1.2 \ --region=us-central1 \ --config=config/config.yaml \ -- \ --data_dir=gs://${BUCKET}/data \ --output_dir=gs://${BUCKET}/${JOB_NAME} \ --train_steps=10000 The preceding command consists of the following elements: ml-engine is a gcloud command group. jobs is an ml-engine command group. submit is a jobs command group. training is a submit command. ${JOB_NAME} is an argument that refers to an environment variable called JOB_NAME that was set earlier. --package-path is a flag set to a path to a Python package to build. -- in isolation separates the gcloud arguments that precede it from the user arguments that follow it. In addition to the term flag, option is often used as a catchall term when you don't want to mire the reader in specialized nomenclature. For more information, see the Cloud SDK: gcloud topic. Linux commands Caution : Linux command syntax is notoriously complex. This section covers only the most common elements. For a more detailed reference, see The Linux Command Line . Where the gcloud CLI uses the catchall terms flag and option, Linux commands use options , parameters , arguments , and a host of specialized syntax elements. The following is an example: find /usr/src/linux -follow -type f -name '*.[ch]' | xargs grep -iHn pcnet The preceding command consists of the following elements: find is the command name. /usr/src/linux is an argument that specifies the path to look in. Easier to refer to as only a path. -follow is an option. The hyphen ( - ), often called a dash in this context, is part of the option. -type is an option with a value of f . -name is an option with a value of '*.[ch]' , where the asterisk ( * ) is a metacharacter signifying a wildcard. Metacharacters are used in Linux shell commands for globbing , or filename expansion. In addition to the asterisk, metacharacters include the question mark ( ? ) and caret ( ^ ). The results of the first command are redirected by using a pipe ( | ) to the xargs grep -iHn pcnet command. Other redirection symbols include the greater than symbol ( > ), less than symbol ( < ), left double angle quotation mark ( << ), and right double angle quotation mark ( >> ). Redirection means capturing output from a file, command, program, script, or even code block within a script and sending it as input to another file, command, program, or script. Linux signals Linux signals require vocabulary choices that are generally discouraged elsewhere in documentation. We recommend using the terms in the following table only in the context of process control: Signal Description SIGKILL Signal sent to kill a specified process, all members of a specified process group, or all processes on the system. SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored. Do not substitute cancel , end , exit , quit , stop , or terminate . SIGTERM Signal sent as a request to terminate a process. Although similar to SIGKILL , this signal gives the process a chance to clean up any child processes that might be running. Do not substitute cancel , end , exit , quit , or stop . SIGQUIT Signal sent from a keyboard to quit a process. Some processes can catch, block, or ignore a quit signal. Do not substitute cancel , end , exit , quit , or stop . SIGINT Signal sent to interrupt a process immediately. The default action of this signal is to terminate a process gracefully. It can be handled, ignored, or caught. It can be sent from a terminal—for example, when a user presses Control+C . Do not substitute suspend , end , exit , pause , or terminate . SIGPAUSE Signal that tells a process to pause , or sleep , until any signal is delivered that either terminates the process or invokes a signal-catching function. Do not substitute cancel or interrupt . SIGSUSPEND Signal sent to temporarily suspend execution of a process. Used to prevent delivery of a particular signal during the execution of a critical code section. Do not substitute pause or exit . SIGSTOP Signal sent to stop execution of a process for later continuation (upon receiving a SIGCONT signal). SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored. Do not substitute cancel , end , exit , interrupt , quit , or terminate .

placeholders.text: This page explains how to format placeholders in commands, code samples, and text strings. This page doesn't explain how to implement visual styling for placeholders, but it does show examples of how Google developer documentation style renders placeholders as visually distinct from other text.
For more information about formatting code, command-line syntax, and code samples, see the following links:
Code in text
Documenting command-line syntax
Code samples

Placeholders in sample code and commands represent values that the reader must replace when they use the sample input. Placeholders in example output can also represent other values that vary. In general, a placeholder has a descriptive name as a default value.
For example, the placeholder PROJECT_ID represents a project ID in sample code, commands, and example output.
In example output, the placeholder HTTP_RESPONSE_CODE represents an HTTP response code; the reader isn't expected to set this to a specific value.

placeholders.heading: Placeholders
placeholders.text: When you create placeholders follow this general guidance around using the letter x :

placeholders.heading: Placeholders
placeholders.text: In general, don't use a single x or a series of x 's as placeholders; use a more informative placeholder.

placeholders.heading: Placeholders
placeholders.text: In some contexts (such as HTTP status codes), a series of x 's is the standard, so it's OK to use (for example) xx in those cases.

placeholders.heading: Placeholders
placeholders.text: There are several ways to format placeholders, depending on whether you're working in HTML or Markdown, or whether the placeholder is inline, in a code block, or in a paragraph. For details, see the following sections.

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: If your sample code and command placeholders occur in a sentence, use the following formatting:

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: In HTML, wrap variable placeholders by using the var element, like this: PLACEHOLDER_NAME

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: PLACEHOLDER_NAME

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: In Markdown, wrap inline placeholders in backticks (`), and use an asterisk (*) before the first backtick and after the second one ( *`PLACEHOLDER_NAME`* ).

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: If your placeholder does not represent a code sample or command, use the following formatting:

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: In HTML, wrap placeholders by using the var element, like this: <var>PLACEHOLDER_NAME</var>

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in inline text
placeholders.text: <var>PLACEHOLDER_NAME</var>

placeholders.heading: Placeholders in code blocks
placeholders.text: If your placeholders are in a block of code, use the following formatting:

placeholders.heading: Explain placeholders
placeholders.text: When you use a placeholder in text or code, explain the placeholder the first time you use it. It's not necessary to repeat the explanation in the document unless doing so might benefit the reader—for example, in circumstances such as the following:

placeholders.heading: Explain placeholders
placeholders.text: Your document is lengthy.

placeholders.heading: Explain placeholders
placeholders.text: You've introduced several other placeholders in a long procedure.

placeholders.heading: Explain placeholders
placeholders.text: Your document isn't intended to be read from beginning to end.

placeholders.heading: Explain placeholders
placeholders.text: The following is an example of a command that uses a placeholder with an explanation of that placeholder:

placeholders.heading: Explain placeholders
placeholders.text:
gcloud compute instances create INSTANCE_NAME \ --metadata enable-guest-attributes=TRUE

Replace INSTANCE_NAME with the name that you want your new VM instance to have.

placeholders.heading: Single placeholder
placeholders.text: Use the following format for a single placeholder:

placeholders.heading: Single placeholder
placeholders.text: Replace PLACEHOLDER with a description of what the placeholder represents.

placeholders.text: Use the following format for two or more placeholders:

placeholders.text:
Tag each placeholder in a code sample or command with code and var elements, followed by a colon and a description that starts with a lowercase letter . For non-code samples, remove the code elements—for example:
  • INSTANCE_NAME: description

placeholders.text: • INSTANCE_NAME: description

If the description contains an example, introduce it with an em dash or such as —for example:

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: When practical, state instructions in terms of what the reader should accomplish, rather than focusing on the widgets and gestures. By avoiding reference to UI elements, you help the reader understand the purpose of an instruction, and it can help future-proof procedures.

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Refresh the page.

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Expand the Advanced options section.

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: However, know the audience and understand the context. In some cases, the point of a procedure is to guide the reader through elements on the page. Or the UI might not be obvious, and it's helpful to explain the gestures for completing a step. Provide the level of detail that seems useful for the intended audience.

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Click Refresh .

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: The rest of this page focuses on scenarios where you've decided it's useful to explicitly discuss UI elements.

ui-elements.heading: Focus on the task
ui-elements.text: For information about writing procedures, see Procedures .

ui-elements.heading: Format names of UI elements
ui-elements.text: When referring to any UI element by name, put its name in bold, using the b element in HTML or ** in Markdown. This includes names for buttons, menus, dialogs, windows, list items, or any other feature on the page that has a visible name. Don't use code font for UI elements, unless it's an element that meets the requirements for code font . In that case, use both code font and bold.

ui-elements.heading: Format names of UI elements
ui-elements.text: Don't make an official feature name or product name bold, except when it directly refers to an element on the page that uses the name (such as a window title or button name).

ui-elements.heading: Format names of UI elements

ui-elements.heading: Format names of UI elements

ui-elements.heading: Format names of UI elements
ui-elements.text: If you document a UI element outside the context of a procedure, try to provide context for the element.

ui-elements.heading: Format names of UI elements

ui-elements.heading: Use appropriate capitalization

ui-elements.heading: Use appropriate capitalization

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: A user interface can contain a variety of UI elements. In general, focus on the feature and its functionality, not the UI element. If you think it adds clarity for the reader, use the name of the UI element. For example, both of the following sentences are valid:

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Go to File > Tools .

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the File menu, click Tools .

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: Don't use slang terms for UI elements—for example, hamburger icon or zippy . For more information, see Buttons and icons .

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: Recommended : To expand the Advanced options section, click the arrow_right expander arrow.

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : To expand the Advanced options section, click the zippy.

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: The following sections define some terms to use when referring to UI elements.

ui-elements.heading: Terminology and usage
ui-elements.text: For prepositions to use with these elements, see the Prepositions table.

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Most often, a window is the entire application window in a desktop environment. However, it can also refer to modular application elements that you can open and close. For example, in Android Studio, several windows are available in the View > Tool Windows menu.

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the MyApp window, click Edit .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : In the MyApp page, click Edit .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Page is the preferred term when referring to a web page in general and to a subpage of a console in particular. For more information, see console .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Google Cloud console, go to the Deployments page.

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : In the Google Cloud console, go to the Deployments window.

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: A dialog is a smaller window that is usually detached from the main application window and appears in front of the window.

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Welcome dialog, click OK .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : In the Welcome pop-up window, click OK .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: A pane (or panel ) is typically a distinct rectangular region within a larger browser or application window. A pane or panel can often be tightly coupled to surrounding UI regions, whereas a window is distinctly separate and can be hidden. Do not use terms such as window , section , area , or column to refer to a pane or panel.

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Create service account pane, click New .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : In the Create service account section, click New .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Create metric pane, do the following:

ui-elements.text: In the Metric type section, select Counter .

ui-elements.heading: Windows, pages, dialogs, panes, and sections
ui-elements.text: In the Labels section, click Add label .

ui-elements.heading: Menus and menu bars
ui-elements.text: In a desktop application, the menu bar appears at the top of the window or at the top of the screen; it's a set of menus (such as File or Edit ), each of which is a set of related commands and/or nested submenus.

ui-elements.heading: Menus and menu bars
ui-elements.text: To refer to an item in a menu, use the term command , not choice , menu item , or option . Exception: if you're documenting how to build an interface, you can use menu item .

ui-elements.heading: Menus and menu bars
ui-elements.text: To refer to a menu, use the form the LABEL_NAME menu.

ui-elements.heading: Menus and menu bars
ui-elements.text: To tell the reader where to find a command in a menu or submenu, use a phrase like In the File menu, select Open .

ui-elements.heading: Menus and menu bars
ui-elements.text: Don't use drop-down as a synonym for menu . See drop-down .

ui-elements.heading: Use angle brackets
ui-elements.text: Another option is to use angle brackets (>). If you use angle brackets, follow these guidelines:

ui-elements.heading: Use angle brackets
ui-elements.text: Put a nonbreaking space (   ) before each angle bracket.

ui-elements.heading: Use angle brackets
ui-elements.text: Don't bold each menu name separately; instead, enclose the entire sequence in a single bold tag ( ... or **...** ).

ui-elements.heading: Use angle brackets
ui-elements.text: Wrap the angle bracket with a span tag and add an aria-label attribute with and then text (for example, > ). Otherwise, some screen readers might read > as "greater than."

ui-elements.heading: Use angle brackets
ui-elements.text: In the following example, the text renders as Select View > Tools > Developer Tools . A screen reader interprets this as Select View and then Tools and then Developer Tools .

ui-elements.heading: HTML
ui-elements.text: Select View&nbsp> Tools&nbsp> Developer Tools.

ui-elements.heading: Markdown
ui-elements.text: Select **View&nbsp> Tools > Developer Tools**.

ui-elements.heading: Markdown
ui-elements.text: This notation is useful for abbreviating a longer phrase like In the File menu, select Open . However, this notation applies only to menu items. Don't use it to describe a combination of different UI elements.

ui-elements.heading: Markdown
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Select MyApp > Preferences , and then select the Languages preference pane.

ui-elements.heading: Markdown
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : Select MyApp > Preferences > Languages > + > CSS .

ui-elements.heading: Navigation menu
ui-elements.text: A navigation menu is a control—usually a pane or window—that contains a list of items that the user can click to go to pages in an application or website. Don't use the terms navigation bar , navigation pane , navigation panel , or navigation window for such a control.

ui-elements.heading: Navigation menu
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the BigQuery navigation menu, click Scheduled queries .

ui-elements.heading: Toolbar
ui-elements.text: A toolbar is a set of buttons for common user actions. A toolbar button that includes a menu is called a menu button . Refer to the toolbar by name if you think that the user needs help finding a button.

ui-elements.heading: Toolbar
ui-elements.text: Recommended : On the Google Cloud console toolbar, click notifications_none Notifications .

ui-elements.heading: Toolbar
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Click notifications_none Notifications .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: A button initiates an action when clicked (or tapped, in the case of a touchscreen). To refer to a button, use the button's label.

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Click OK .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : Click the "OK" button.

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: An icon is a symbol or image that represents an object or a function. An icon can be a button as well. If the button includes an icon, write the name of the button as shown in the tooltip, and add the button icon before the name. If you need to use a space between the icon and the name for readability, use a nonbreaking space.

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Click more_vert Settings and utilities .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : Click more_vert .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: If the icon tooltip is identical to the name of the icon, use an empty alt attribute .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: If you're unsure of the name of the icon, inspect the element using browser tools. In many cases, a visual element like an icon has an ARIA attribute that provides a textual description of the element for use by screen readers. To inspect an element, right-click the element and select Inspect or Inspect element , depending on your browser. Look for one of the following types of labels: aria-labelledby , aria-label , aria-describedby , label , placeholder , or title . For more information, see Using aria-label and Accessible Name and Description calculation .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: If a button with an icon doesn't include a tooltip, submit a bug report requesting that a tooltip be added. Tooltips are crucial for accessibility, and for documentation and discoverability in general.

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Click Add .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : Click the icon.

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: If a UI element name ends with an ellipsis (...), leave out the ellipsis.

ui-elements.text: Recommended : Click Browse .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Not recommended : Click Browse ... .

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons
ui-elements.text: Don't use directional language to orient the reader, such as above , below , or right-hand side . Phrases like those don't work well for accessibility or for localization. If a UI element is hard to find, provide a screenshot.

ui-elements.heading: Buttons and icons

ui-elements.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
ui-elements.text: If you have UI elements that are difficult to find, consider one of the following options as an alternative to using directional language, which can be problematic for accessibility and localization reasons.

ui-elements.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
ui-elements.text: Use the button icon along with its name as shown in the button tooltip. Recommended : Click refresh Refresh .

ui-elements.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
ui-elements.text: Add context to help the user find the element. Recommended : On the Cloud Run toolbar, click refresh Refresh .

ui-elements.heading: Difficult-to-find UI elements
ui-elements.text: Use a screenshot. Recommended : In the list of services, click view_column Column display options . For more information about when and how to use screenshots, see Diagrams, figures, and other images .

ui-elements.heading: Tab
ui-elements.text: A tab is a navigation element that looks like a file tab. To refer to a tab, use the form the LABEL_NAME tab .

ui-elements.heading: Tab
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Select Tools > Options , and then click the Edit tab.

ui-elements.heading: Text box
ui-elements.text: A text box is a box that the user can type in. Use box and the form the LABEL_NAME box . Format the text that the user types by using the code element in HTML, or by using code formatting (monospace) in other markup.

ui-elements.heading: Text box
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Owner box, enter your name.

ui-elements.heading: Text box
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Name box, enter wsfc-1 .

ui-elements.heading: Text box
ui-elements.text: In Google Cloud, use field instead of box .

ui-elements.heading: Text box
ui-elements.text: In Google Workspace documentation, use field instead of box .

ui-elements.heading: Text box
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Instance field, specify a value less than 64 characters long.

ui-elements.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
ui-elements.text: A list box is a box that offers the user a list of items. To refer to a list box, use the form the LABEL_NAME list or the LABEL_NAME box , whichever is clearer.

ui-elements.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Item list, select Desktop .

ui-elements.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
ui-elements.text: A combo box is a combination of a text box and a list box. To refer to a combo box, use the form the LABEL_NAME box . To refer to entering a value into a combo box, use the verbs type or select or enter .

ui-elements.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Font box, type or select the font that you want to use.

ui-elements.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
ui-elements.text: A spin box is a box that lets the user choose a value by clicking arrows or by typing. To refer to a spin box, use the form the LABEL_NAME box . To refer to entering a value into a spin box, use the verb enter .

ui-elements.heading: List box, combo box, and spin box
ui-elements.text: Recommended : In the Font Size box, enter a font size.

ui-elements.heading: Checkbox
ui-elements.text: A checkbox is a small box that indicates whether an option is on or off. To refer to a checkbox, use the form the LABEL_NAME checkbox .

ui-elements.heading: Checkbox
ui-elements.text: Be wary of using the verbs check and uncheck , which can be ambiguous; it's often best to use select and clear instead.

ui-elements.heading: Checkbox
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Select the Automatically check for updates checkbox.

ui-elements.heading: Checkbox
ui-elements.text: Recommended : Clear the Bookmarks checkbox.

ui-elements.heading: Checkbox
ui-elements.text: If you need to refer to the state of the checkbox, it's often best to refer to it as selected or not selected . Recommended : Make sure that the Bookmarks checkbox is selected. Recommended : Make sure that the Bookmarks checkbox isn't selected. Radio button A radio button is a small button used to choose one item from a group of mutually exclusive options. To refer to a radio button, use the radio button's label, or refer to the group of buttons by its label. Recommended : Select Do not remember passwords . Recommended : For Startup mode , select an option. Expander arrow An expander arrow is the UI element used to expand or collapse a section of navigation or content.
